draft.title: [bug]: Make solution start same-origin and surface connection failures
draft.body:
## Summary

`bifrost solution start` injects its internal loopback URL into the browser bundle. When an outer development proxy such as Codex forwards a different browser-visible port or hostname to that loopback listener, the page loads successfully but subsequent API and WebSocket calls bypass the outer proxy. The SDK header then swallows the failed identity request and displays `Account`, leaving a plausible-looking but unauthenticated app.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Run `bifrost solution start` on its loopback listener.
2. Access it through a forwarding proxy that exposes a different browser origin or port.
3. Observe that the app shell loads but identity/API calls target the injected internal loopback origin.
4. Observe the header falling back to `Account` instead of explaining the connection failure.

## Expected behavior

- Browser API and WebSocket traffic under `solution start` uses the successful browser origin and rides through the local Bifrost proxy.
- The local proxy remains the single origin for Vite, local workflows, and the upstream Bifrost API.
- `--host` remains available for binding another interface but is unrelated to forwarded-origin routing.
- Authentication or connectivity failures show an actionable diagnostic state instead of rendering the app as `Account`.

## Actual behavior

The bundle receives an absolute `http://127.0.0.1:<port>` API URL. A forwarded browser origin therefore makes cross-origin or unreachable requests, and `BifrostHeader` silently reduces all failures to `Account`.

## Notes

POC scope:
- make the `solution start` transport same-origin;
- reuse or extract the existing standalone-app diagnostic state before rendering the app;
- preserve `--host` and existing direct-access behavior;
- cover forwarded-origin routing, authentication failures, HTTP APIs, and WebSockets with tests.

draft.title: Fork-based process pool leaks zombie children until the worker can no longer fork()
draft.body:
## Summary

The execution process pool leaks a zombie process on **every** workflow execution. The template process (`template_process.py`) `os.fork()`s a child per execution but never reaps it, and the reap code that does exist (`_PidWrapper` in `process_pool.py`) runs in the wrong process to ever succeed. Under sustained execution volume the worker container accumulates defunct processes until it hits the PID/`RLIMIT_NPROC` ceiling, at which point the template can no longer `fork()` and every execution routed to it fails.

This is the same underlying bug that #243 tried to fix and #293 reverted. This issue documents the root cause precisely and — importantly — why a naive reap re-triggers the #293 crash storm, so the follow-up fix can be landed safely.

## Symptoms (self-hosted deployment)

After ~27h of worker uptime under normal load:

- Worker logs, repeating:
  - `[pool] Batch install error ([Errno 11] Resource temporarily unavailable: '/usr/local/bin/python')`
  - `BlockingIOError: [Errno 11] Resource temporarily unavailable`
  - `src.services.execution.process_pool - ERROR - Template process died — restarting`
  - Every workflow execution then fails with `EOFError` (broken pipe to the dead template). ~76 template deaths in 6h once it tips over.
- Inside the worker container: **~19,000 processes in state `Z` (defunct)**. `docker exec … sh -c 'ps'` fails with `Cannot fork`.
- Host memory and disk are fine — this is pure PID/zombie exhaustion, not OOM.

Reproduce the zombie count on the host:

```bash
ps -e -o stat= | grep -c Z          # climbs by ~1 per execution, never drops
docker stats <worker> --no-stream --format 'PIDs={{.PIDs}}'
```

Mitigation is a worker restart (zombies reparent to init and clear), but the leak simply rebuilds.

## Root cause

The fast-fork pool: a long-lived **template process** (spawned via `multiprocessing`) preloads deps, then `os.fork()`s a fresh child per execution. The child runs one execution and calls `os._exit(0)` (`_run_forked_child`).

1. **The template never reaps its children.** `template_process.py` has no `waitpid`, no `SIGCHLD` handler, no reap loop. `_handle_fork_request` (`template_process.py:272`) forks, sends the `child_pid` back to the consumer, and returns to the fork loop (`template_process.py:245`). When each non-persistent child exits, it becomes a **zombie parented to the template**.

2. **The reap code that exists is in the wrong process.** `_PidWrapper.join()` / `is_alive()` (`process_pool.py:216`) call `os.waitpid(self.pid, …)` — but they run in the **main worker process**, and the fork children are its *grandchildren* (children of the template). `waitpid` on a non-child raises `ChildProcessError` (ECHILD), which is caught and ignored. So the main process never reaps them, and the template — which could — doesn't try.

Net: one leaked zombie per execution, monotonically, until `fork()` returns `EAGAIN`.

## Why the naive fix (#243) caused the #293 crash storm — and why it's still a trap

#243 (91d9dffb) added `os.waitpid(WNOHANG)` inside `_PidWrapper.is_alive()`. Because that runs in the main process where ECHILD is the *normal* result, ECHILD was misread as "child exited cleanly," so `is_alive()` returned `False` while executions were still running → `_check_process_health` declared them crashed → crash storm (reverted in #293).

But there is a second, subtler trap that survives even if you move the reap to the correct process:

**The un-reaped zombie is currently load-bearing.** `_PidWrapper.is_alive()` is `os.kill(pid, 0)`, and a zombie still answers `kill(pid,0)` as alive. In `_check_process_health` (`process_pool.py:1135`), Case A is:

```python
if not handle.is_alive and handle.state != ProcessState.KILLED:
    # unexpected crash
    if handle.current_execution and not handle.result_reported:
        await self._report_crash(handle)
```

So today, a just-finished child stays "alive" (as a zombie) until the result loop drains its result and sets `result_reported`. That zombie is what prevents Case A from firing during the normal completion window. **Reap the child — even correctly, in the template — and `is_alive` flips to `False` the instant it exits, re-exposing a completion-vs-crash race: if the health check runs after exit but before the result is drained, it declares a false crash.** Same storm, different door.

## Suggested fix (two coupled parts)

Both are needed together; either alone is unsafe.

1. **Reap in the template's fork loop** (the real parent), not in `is_alive()`. e.g. a non-blocking sweep each loop iteration:

   ```python
   def _reap_children() -> None:
       while True:
           try:
               pid, _ = os.waitpid(-1, os.WNOHANG)
           except ChildProcessError:
               break
           if pid == 0:
               break
   ```

   The template loop already wakes every 1s (`pipe.poll(timeout=1.0)`), so this bounds zombie lifetime to ~1s. During the fork loop the template runs no `subprocess` (pip install happens once at load, before the loop), so `waitpid(-1)` won't steal a subprocess child.

2. **Make `_check_process_health` Case A tolerant of a reaped-but-result-pending child** — drain the handle's result queue (and/or honor a short grace window keyed off first-observed-exit) before declaring a crash, so a completed child whose result is still in flight is reported as success, not `ProcessCrashError`. (This is the legitimate half of #243 that #293 rolled back alongside the broken `is_alive` sampling.)

Guardrails learned from #293: never sample `waitpid` in `is_alive()`; never treat ECHILD as "clean exit" (it only means "not my child / already reaped").

## Acceptance / repro (from #293)

```bash
for i in $(seq 1 30); do bifrost workflows execute crash_repro & done
```

- Before a correct fix: crashes / "no idle process" cascades (with the naive reap), or a steadily climbing zombie count (current `main`).
- After: **0 `ProcessCrashError`**, and `ps -e -o stat= | grep -c Z` stays flat across repeated runs.

## Affected code

- `api/src/services/execution/template_process.py` — `_handle_fork_request` (`:272`), fork loop (`:245`), `os.fork()` (`:298`); no reaping anywhere.
- `api/src/services/execution/process_pool.py` — `_PidWrapper` (`:216`), `_check_process_health` Case A (`:1135`).

Present on `main` HEAD. Prior art: #243 (91d9dffb), reverted by #293 (8ae87b82).

draft.title: Harden agent delegation lifecycle without changing tool schemas
draft.body:
## Problem

Agent delegation already exposes a simple task-only tool, but autonomous and chat execution do not share one reliable lifecycle contract. Some child terminal states can be returned to the parent as a normal empty result, cancellation and unexpected exceptions can leave incomplete run state, and caller context / nested ancestry need explicit guarantees.

## Approach

- Keep every delegate_to_<agent> tool and its required task string input unchanged.
- Introduce one internal structured delegation outcome containing status, output, error, and child run ID.
- Give delegated work a durable child run and terminalize it on success, failure, timeout, cancellation, pause, budget exhaustion, or unexpected exception.
- Ensure the parent always receives an explicit child result or error unless the parent itself is cancelled.
- Preserve caller and organization context across delegation.
- Preserve nested parent/child ancestry and propagate cancellation through the delegation tree.
- Flush child steps and usage consistently.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Existing delegation tool names and JSON Schema remain byte-for-byte compatible.
- [ ] Autonomous and chat delegation use the same status/result semantics.
- [ ] Completed, failed, timed-out, cancelled, paused, budget-exceeded, and unexpected-exception children all reach explicit durable terminal outcomes.
- [ ] Parents receive child failures as errors rather than normal None/empty output.
- [ ] Nested delegation ancestry is persisted and queryable.
- [ ] Caller identity and organization boundaries survive delegation.
- [ ] Parent/root cancellation stops active descendants.
- [ ] Child steps and AI usage are flushed on every terminal path.
- [ ] Unit and E2E tests cover the lifecycle matrix, nesting, cancellation, caller context, and schema compatibility.
- [ ] A low-cost OpenRouter model completes a real delegation round trip.

## Out of scope

Parallel sibling execution and public agent/tool contract changes. Those can follow once lifecycle correctness is established.

draft.title: [feature]: Replace global MCP tool aggregation with an agent gateway
draft.body:
## Problem

The default `/mcp` endpoint can expose 100+ tools by flattening every tool available through every agent the caller can access. This bloats model context, loses agent-specific instructions and provenance, and depends on MCP clients refreshing cached tool catalogs whenever agents or workflows evolve.

The per-agent `/mcp/{agent_id}` endpoint provides the native schema-rich experience and should remain available.

## Proposed solution

Replace the default `/mcp` tool surface with four stable gateway tools:

- `bifrost_find_agents`
- `bifrost_get_agent`
- `bifrost_get_tool_schema`
- `bifrost_execute_tool`

The gateway should:

- Search only agents visible to the authenticated caller.
- Return live agent instructions and compact tool summaries.
- Fetch full schemas lazily for one selected tool.
- Execute through an agent-bound stable tool reference rather than a globally ambiguous tool name.
- Re-resolve access and validate parameters against the live schema on every execution.
- Return structured validation errors that a model can repair.
- Preserve `/mcp/{agent_id}` with its current native tool-list and initialization behavior.

The proof of concept will not require an `expected_revision` handshake. Live authorization, resolution, and schema validation at execution time are sufficient unless testing demonstrates a concrete stale-read race that needs another guard.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Default `/mcp` exposes only the four gateway tools.
- [ ] `bifrost_find_agents` supports task-oriented search and returns only accessible agents.
- [ ] `bifrost_get_agent` returns live instructions and compact tool summaries with stable agent-bound references.
- [ ] `bifrost_get_tool_schema` returns the selected tool's exact live input schema and useful metadata.
- [ ] `bifrost_execute_tool` reauthorizes the agent/tool tuple, validates parameters, dispatches through the canonical execution path, and records resolved provenance.
- [ ] Agent system, workflow, delegation, knowledge, and external MCP tool sources are handled consistently with the native agent resolver, or any intentional proof-of-concept exclusions are documented and tested.
- [ ] Invalid parameters return structured, model-repairable errors.
- [ ] Existing `/mcp/{agent_id}` behavior remains unchanged.
- [ ] Unit and MCP E2E tests cover discovery, authorization, schema lookup, execution, and invalid parameters.
- [ ] A debug-stack experiment demonstrates discovery and successful execution with a cheap OpenRouter model such as DeepSeek V4 Pro.
- [ ] The experiment reports latency, gateway call count, schema-retry behavior, and observed failure modes.

## Design doc link (optional)

A focused implementation plan/spec will be added under `docs/superpowers/specs/` during the proof of concept.

draft.title: [feature]: Standardize durable platform jobs
draft.body:
## Summary

Bifrost has accumulated several incompatible implementations of long-running
platform work:

- application publishing
- embedding reindexing
- Solution backup export
- Solution deploy/install
- git operations and workspace reimport
- summary-backfill orchestration

They currently differ in persistence, execution location, status vocabulary,
progress delivery, cancellation, timeout handling, retry behavior, and recovery
after an API/scheduler/container crash. New features should not have to invent
another job table, polling loop, WebSocket protocol, or stale-job cleanup path.

Introduce a standardized, scheduler-owned durable platform-job kernel and use
asynchronous application publishing as its first handler. Migrate the remaining
long-running operations through independently mergeable follow-up PRs.

## Production bug motivating the work

On 2026-07-27, publishing an existing inline_v1 application through
`POST /api/applications/{app_id}/publish` exceeded the CLI's hard-coded
30-second HTTP timeout. The CLI reported a blank error while the API continued
processing for roughly two minutes and ultimately published successfully.

Application publishing must enqueue quickly, preserve build-before-promotion,
and expose durable progress and errors after the initiating request ends.

## Goals

- One durable PostgreSQL source of truth for platform-job lifecycle state.
- One formal status/progress/error/result contract shared by HTTP and WebSocket.
- Scheduler-owned execution; workflow and agent execution workers remain
  execution-only.
- No additional container.
- Atomic claiming with leases, heartbeats, fencing, and stale-claim recovery.
- Explicit handler policies for timeout, retry, cancellation, deduplication,
  concurrency, and resource requirements.
- Global and per-handler concurrency limits.
- Cgroup memory-headroom admission before starting resource-intensive work.
- UI uses the existing WebSocket connection and Notification Center rather than
  polling.
- CLI can poll the same durable snapshot endpoint using short HTTP requests.
- A typed, versioned handler/payload interface flexible enough for later
  migrations without adding new lifecycle infrastructure.
- Durable state survives API, scheduler, Redis, and container restarts.

## Non-goals

- Do not move workflow or agent execution into the platform-job system.
- Do not add a new platform-job container.
- Do not force short, idempotent cron housekeeping into durable jobs unless it
  needs caller-visible progress, cancellation, retries, or results.
- Do not migrate every existing job in the first PR.

## Proposed handler contract

Each job type registers a typed/versioned payload and result plus declarative
policy:

- timeout
- maximum attempts and retry-on-runner-loss behavior
- deduplication scope/key
- maximum concurrency
- minimum memory headroom
- cancellation support

The runner supplies a common context for progress reporting, cancellation
checks, heartbeat/lease management, and terminal result/error persistence.

## Delivery plan

- [ ] **PR 1 — Standardized platform jobs + application publishing**
  - Add the generic durable job model, service, contracts, handler registry,
    scheduler processor, leases/heartbeats/fencing, resource admission, cleanup,
    and WebSocket projection.
  - Replace the app-specific publish-job implementation with the first generic
    handler.
  - Return `202` immediately, deduplicate active publishes, preserve
    build-before-promotion, and publish the live manifest last.
  - Update UI, Notification Center, CLI, MCP, generated contracts, and tests.
  - Cover enqueue, subscription, polling, success, bundle failure, duplicate
    publish, timeout, scheduler loss, lease recovery, and resource deferral.

- [ ] **PR 2 — Embedding reindex**
  - Replace Redis pub/sub dispatch and notification-as-job-record state.
  - Adopt generic progress/cancellation while preserving partial/resumable
    behavior.

- [ ] **PR 3 — Solution backup export**
  - Replace duplicated export-job lifecycle handling.
  - Exercise artifact metadata, encrypted parameters, retention, expiration,
    and cleanup.

- [ ] **PR 4 — Solution deploy/install**
  - Remove FastAPI `BackgroundTasks`.
  - Adopt durable dispatch, resource locking, and explicit deploy retry and
    idempotency rules.

- [ ] **PR 5 — Git operations and workspace reimport**
  - Remove ephemeral Redis dispatch/results and migrate conflict/action-required
    outcomes to the shared contract.

- [ ] **PR 6 — Summary backfill and remaining audit**
  - Standardize parent orchestration while leaving execution-related child work
    in the execution workers.
  - Audit remaining long-running maintenance operations and migrate those that
    require durability or observability.

## PR 1 acceptance criteria

- The original synchronous application-publish timeout is fixed without
  weakening build-before-promotion.
- No app-specific lifecycle table, status enum, polling protocol, or stale-job
  processor remains.
- A scheduler/container crash cannot leave a job permanently running.
- Low memory prevents new resource-intensive jobs from starting without losing
  them.
- Repeated publish requests reuse the active operation.
- The browser receives progress and terminal state through WebSocket.
- CLI callers can reliably follow the durable operation beyond the per-request
  HTTP timeout.
- Errors and progress remain queryable after the initiating request exits.
- Tests demonstrate that a second handler can use the kernel without adding new
  lifecycle infrastructure.

## Compatibility

The application publish response changes from an immediate application object
to `202 Accepted` plus a durable job identifier. Update the contract version and
all first-party CLI, MCP, and UI consumers in PR 1. Later migrations must state
their compatibility impact independently.

draft.title: [feature]: SSO-only login enforcement with a break-glass fallback path
draft.body:
## Problem

Bifrost supports password, passkey (WebAuthn), and SSO (Microsoft/Google/OIDC) login, but there is no way to turn password or passkey auth off. Orgs with a mandated IdP can't enforce it: every user retains a password/passkey path that bypasses IdP conditional access and deprovisioning — disable an employee in the IdP and their Bifrost password still works.

The scaffolding exists but was never finished:

- `api/src/routers/auth.py:1347` — `password_login_enabled=True,  # Always enabled for now`, hardcoded in the public `/auth/status` response.
- The contract field (`api/src/models/contracts/auth.py:34`) is plumbed to generated TS types but **nothing reads it** — `Login.tsx:489` branches only on `oauthProviders.length > 0`; the password form renders unconditionally and the passkey button is gated only by browser support (`Login.tsx:75`).

An emergent, per-user version already exists: `hashed_password` is nullable (`models/orm/users.py:34`) and `/auth/login` rejects passwordless users (`auth.py:336-349`). But it's implicit and silently undone the moment the user sets a password via `PUT /profile/password` (`profile.py:247`), which explicitly allows passkey/OAuth users to set one.

The counterpart problem is why this can't be a plain kill switch: if SSO breaks (expired client secret, IdP outage, misconfiguration), everyone is locked out, and first-run bootstrap (`needs_setup` → first user becomes PlatformAdmin) runs through the password path. Enforcement needs a recovery route.

## Proposed solution

Two halves; neither is safe alone.

**1. Global policy + server-side enforcement.** A global setting for allowed login methods (SSO login config is already global — `system_configs` with `organization_id IS NULL`, `oauth_config_service.py:81` — so a global policy matches the existing model; `BIFROST_MFA_ENABLED` in `config.py` is the pattern to mirror, or store DB-side next to the SSO config). Per-org policy is explicitly out of scope — it would require per-org SSO provider config first.

Enforce at every affected endpoint — hiding the form is not a boundary:

| Surface | Endpoints |
|---|---|
| Password login | `POST /auth/login` (`auth.py:282`), `POST /auth/mfa/login` (`:661`), `POST /auth/mfa/verify` (`:539`, returns tokens — defense-in-depth; its `mfa_token` is only minted by `/auth/login`) |
| Password creation | `POST /auth/register` (`:1172`), `POST /auth/register-from-invite` (`:1826`), `PUT /profile/password` (`profile.py:247` — "set password" for passkey/OAuth users) |
| Passkey login | `POST /passkeys/authenticate/options` (`passkeys.py:133`), `POST /passkeys/authenticate/verify` (`:166`) |
| Passkey enrollment | `POST /passkeys/register/options\|verify` (`passkeys.py:50`, `:81`), `POST /auth/setup/passkey/*` (`auth.py:1576`, `:1637`), invite passkey variants (`:1852`, `:1874`) |

Explicitly **not** gated: the device flow. `POST /auth/device/token` only polls a `device_code`; authorization happens at `/auth/device/authorize` behind an existing authenticated session (`auth.py:1728`), so CLI login via device flow remains SSO-compatible. (The CLI's direct password flow, `api/bifrost/cli.py:432`, is covered by the `/auth/login` gate.) There is also no forgot-password/email-reset flow in the codebase — nothing extra to gate there.

Wire `/auth/status` to real values (add a passkey field alongside `password_login_enabled`) and make `Login.tsx` consume both.

**2. Break-glass path.** A non-default URL (e.g. `/login/recovery`) permitting password/passkey when the normal flow is SSO-only:

- Not linked from the login page, not advertised via `/auth/status`.
- Restricted to platform admins (`is_platform_admin`) — no per-user eligibility flag.
- Every use emits an audit event (`emit_audit` pattern already throughout `auth.py`) — break-glass should be loud.
- Stricter rate limit than normal login.
- **MFA required even when `mfa_enabled` is false** — `/auth/login` currently issues tokens immediately with no second factor when MFA is globally off (`auth.py:385-389`); break-glass must not inherit that.

**Guard rails** (precedent: `oauth_sso.py:503-512` already blocks unlinking a user's last OAuth account when they have no password — this is the inverse):

- Refuse to enable SSO-only unless ≥1 SSO provider is fully configured (`get_available_providers`, `oauth_config_service.py:325`).
- Refuse to remove/unconfigure the last SSO provider while SSO-only is active.
- First-run setup stays reachable.
- Decide/document session semantics: enabling SSO-only does **not** retroactively kill live password-derived sessions — `POST /auth/refresh` keeps them alive. Either revoke on flip or document `/auth/revoke-all` / `/auth/admin/revoke-user` (`auth.py:1075`, `:1119`) as the follow-up step.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A global setting controls permitted login methods (password, passkey, SSO)
- [ ] `GET /auth/status` returns real values for password and passkey availability; no hardcoded literals
- [ ] `Login.tsx` hides the password form and passkey button based on `/auth/status`
- [ ] Every endpoint in the enforcement table rejects disabled methods server-side with a clear error, covered by e2e tests hitting the API directly
- [ ] `PUT /profile/password` and passkey enrollment are gated consistently with the login policy
- [ ] CLI device flow still works under SSO-only (browser authorization via SSO)
- [ ] Break-glass URL permits password/passkey login for platform admins only; non-admins rejected
- [ ] Break-glass logins emit an audit event, require MFA regardless of `mfa_enabled`, and have a stricter rate limit
- [ ] SSO-only cannot be enabled with no fully-configured SSO provider; last provider cannot be removed while active
- [ ] First-run setup works with SSO-only configured
- [ ] Enabling SSO-only either revokes existing password-derived sessions or the docs state the manual revocation step
- [ ] Backend unit + e2e tests in `api/tests/`; Playwright happy-path spec in `client/e2e/` for SSO-only login page + break-glass
- [ ] Docs cover enabling SSO-only and break-glass recovery during an SSO outage

## Design doc link (optional)

None yet — warrants one at `docs/superpowers/specs/` given the auth surface and lockout risk.

draft.title: [feature]: Consolidate MCP capability discovery and add optional async execution
draft.body:
## Summary

Consolidate the default Bifrost MCP gateway into progressive capability discovery with optional asynchronous workflow execution.

Replace the current four-tool unscoped gateway with:

- `bifrost_search_capabilities`
- `bifrost_execute_tool` with a model-facing `async=false` override
- `bifrost_get_execution`

Keep `/mcp/{agent_id}` unchanged.

## Capability discovery contract

Search agents and their agent-bound tools while keeping the complete catalog server-side.

- Results expose `matching_tools`, never a field that implies a complete tool catalog.
- Every returned agent reports `total_tools`, `returned_tools`, and `complete`.
- A zero-match result must explicitly state that absence from the projection does not mean the agent lacks the capability.
- Partial results include machine-readable and textual guidance to search again with `agent_id` and a narrower capability description.
- Agent instructions that mention an undiscovered capability should lead the caller to search again within that agent.
- Search responses stop before a serialized-size budget, preserve valid structured JSON, and report omitted matches.
- Full input schemas are loaded only for selected tools through progressive discovery.

## Execution contract

- `bifrost_execute_tool` remains synchronous by default.
- For workflow-backed tools, `async=true` enqueues the existing workflow execution and immediately returns its Bifrost execution ID.
- Unsupported sources return a structured `ASYNC_NOT_SUPPORTED` error rather than ignoring the override.
- `bifrost_get_execution` returns an ownership-checked, compact status/result projection.
- Newly queued Redis-only executions are visible to their initiating user before the worker creates the PostgreSQL row.
- Large execution results use a bounded, valid structured response rather than truncated JSON.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Default `/mcp tools/list` exposes exactly seven stable tools: required instructions, three memory operations, capability search, execute, and get execution.
- [ ] Search ranks accessible agents and agent-bound tools.
- [ ] Every agent result clearly distinguishes matching tools from its complete catalog.
- [ ] Partial and zero-tool results explicitly instruct the caller how to discover more.
- [ ] Search output obeys count and serialized-size budgets without invalid JSON.
- [ ] Selected tool schemas and live agent instructions can be hydrated progressively.
- [ ] Existing authorization, allow/block configuration, stable references, and live revocation checks remain enforced.
- [ ] Synchronous execution remains the default and preserves existing behavior.
- [ ] `async=true` immediately returns an execution ID for workflow tools.
- [ ] `bifrost_get_execution` enforces execution ownership and returns bounded result data.
- [ ] `/mcp/{agent_id}` remains unchanged.
- [ ] Focused unit and MCP E2E tests cover discovery completeness, refinement, authorization, sync execution, async execution, pending lookup, completion, and bounded output.

Follow-up to #528.

draft.title: [bug]: Reconnect Web SDK subscriptions after transient socket closure
draft.body:
## Summary
Standalone v2 apps lose execution, table, and file realtime subscriptions when the API restarts or a deployment closes WebSockets with code 1012. The SDK logs the close but does not reconnect.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Open a standalone v2 app using useWorkflow and useTable.
2. Restart or deploy the API while the tab remains open.
3. Observe execution stream closed 1012 and table subscription closed 1012 in the console.

## Expected behavior
Transient closures reconnect with bounded exponential backoff, resubscribe automatically, and reconcile missed table/file state. Explicit unsubscribe and authorization/policy failures do not reconnect.

## Actual behavior
The socket is one-shot. Execution falls back to polling, while table/file updates stop until the app reloads.

## Acceptance criteria
- Execution, table, and file streams reconnect after transient closes.
- Successful reconnect resets backoff and resubscribes once.
- Table/file hooks refresh their snapshot after reconnect.
- Execution polling remains available during an outage.
- Unsubscribe cancels pending reconnects; 4001/4003 do not loop.
- The Bifrost build skill explains when and how to run solution sdk update for existing apps.
- Focused SDK tests cover 1012, unsubscribe, auth failure, and reconciliation.

## Environment
Observed in DMARC Management on bifrost.gocovi.com during a platform deployment.

## Notes
One deployment-resilience PR may close this together with the execution read-after-create and stale hosted-asset issues.

draft.title: [bug]: Return Pending for executions still in Redis before PostgreSQL creation
draft.body:
## Summary
POST /api/workflows/execute returns an execution ID before the worker creates its PostgreSQL row. Immediate GET /api/executions/{id} therefore returns transient 404 responses even though the execution was just accepted and exists in Redis.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Start an asynchronous workflow through the web SDK.
2. Immediately GET the returned execution ID while the worker has not created the database row.
3. Observe one or more 404 responses before the row appears.

## Expected behavior
A returned execution ID is immediately readable. PostgreSQL remains authoritative; on a database miss, the detail endpoint checks the owned Redis pending record and returns a contract-valid Pending execution. A missing record in both stores remains 404.

## Actual behavior
The REST detail endpoint checks only PostgreSQL. Client retry logic masks the race but still emits visible 404 requests.

## Acceptance criteria
- GET checks PostgreSQL first and preserves all existing completed/running behavior.
- On DB miss only, an authorized Redis pending record returns status Pending.
- Unauthorized pending executions remain hidden with the existing authorization semantics.
- Missing from both stores still returns 404.
- No changes to enqueue, worker startup, cancellation, or execution persistence semantics.
- Tests hold the worker boundary and prove immediate read-after-create without 404.

## Environment
Observed in DMARC Management on bifrost.gocovi.com using the standalone v2 web SDK.

## Notes
The MCP gateway already implements a DB-first Redis fallback; REST should use a shared, contract-correct version of that established behavior.

draft.title: [bug]: Recover hosted apps when deployed bundle assets become stale
draft.body:
## Summary
An already-open hosted app can retain old hashed JavaScript or CSS URLs after a deployment removes those assets. StandaloneV2App manually injects module scripts and stylesheets, so these failures bypass the host clients Vite preload-error recovery. A missing stylesheet can leave the application visibly unstyled until manual refresh.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Keep a hosted standalone v2 app tab open.
2. Deploy a new app bundle that replaces hashed entry/CSS assets.
3. Return to or remount the old tab after an obsolete asset is requested.

## Expected behavior
The host waits for required entry and stylesheet assets, revalidates the bundle manifest after a stale-asset failure, and mounts the current bundle without manual refresh. Genuine current-bundle failures surface once without a reload loop.

## Actual behavior
Entry failures become a static error and stylesheet failures are not handled, allowing unstyled rendering.

## Acceptance criteria
- Entry JS and CSS are both treated as required before mounting.
- Asset failure triggers one uncached manifest revalidation.
- Changed hashes remount the current bundle without full-page refresh.
- Unchanged broken hashes surface an actionable error and do not loop.
- Component tests cover JS failure, CSS failure, recovery, and loop guard.
- A targeted Playwright test reproduces stale assets against a debug stack and captures screenshot evidence of the recovered styled app.

Observed in DMARC Management on bifrost.gocovi.com after deployment.

draft.title: [chore]: Build a reliable layered test and artifact pipeline
draft.body:
## What

Build a reliable layered test and artifact pipeline for Bifrost while preserving the complete exact-candidate merge gate that protects the shared `:dev` image.

The program has five explicit layers:

1. Fast pull-request feedback: lint, type/contract checks, backend unit tests, and client Vitest.
2. Exact merge-candidate protection: the complete current backend integration/E2E suite, plus a deliberately small and reliable critical-browser smoke set.
3. Shared dev publication: test the production candidate before publication, promote an immutable tested digest, deploy it, and verify application-level smoke checks.
4. Nightly discovery: full Playwright, clean/uncached builds, upgrade/migration validation, randomized-order/state-leak exposure, and scheduler/worker concurrency or soak coverage.
5. Release validation: validate the release artifact, version/manifests, compatibility, install/upgrade, signing/attestation, and deployment smoke without blindly repeating identical source checks.

Perform an in-depth test-by-test reliability review. Permanently repair supported instances of product races, leaked state, incorrect synchronization/eventual-consistency assumptions, nondeterministic fixtures, resource contention, brittle harness contracts, and overcomplicated or redundant tests. Keep each unique behavioral signal at the lowest durable layer.

## Why

The existing 61-day analysis covered 737 Actions runs and found repeated 20–25 minute broad-suite execution plus recurring timing/state failures. The evidence points primarily to product/test synchronization and state isolation defects, not generic Docker instability. Known examples include Redis cleanup/state leakage, pending-delivery worker races, Redis-to-PostgreSQL eventual consistency in form embed startup, authentication expiry cascades, exact migration-head assumptions, and raw WebSocket timing.

The current topology also has architectural gaps:

- Full backend E2E is now correctly deferred from ordinary PRs to the exact merge candidate, but many backend "unit" tests still pay for a complete Docker stack.
- Playwright is not currently part of GitHub Actions.
- The suite tests development/test images, after which `main` builds fresh production images for `:dev`; the exact published digest is not exercised by the suite.
- Dev deployment verifies Kubernetes rollout status but not login/API/core-product behavior.
- Version tags repeat the complete source gate and then build another fresh set of production images.
- There is no nightly upgrade, concurrency/soak, randomized-order, or state-leak discovery program.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The complete current required suite continues to pass against the exact merge candidate before any commit can produce the shared `:dev` image, unless replaced by an objectively equivalent or stronger exact-artifact gate.
- [ ] Direct-to-main or other publication paths cannot bypass the proven gate; repository settings are not weakened.
- [ ] The historical report and architecture plan document methodology, limitations, ownership, test taxonomy, safety invariants, and measured baselines.
- [ ] Highest-frequency failing tests/areas receive evidence-backed root-cause categories and durable fixes or justified simplification/deletion with replacement coverage identified.
- [ ] No retries, rerun-until-green behavior, skip/xfail/quarantine, blanket timeout inflation, or swallowed failures are introduced.
- [ ] Pure tests no longer require the full Docker stack where a lower test layer preserves the same signal.
- [ ] A small reliable critical Playwright smoke set protects the exact merge candidate.
- [ ] The complete Playwright suite and other expensive discovery checks run on a scheduled nightly workflow with clear ownership and retained diagnostics.
- [ ] Production-candidate images are exercised before shared publication, are signed/attested, and are promoted by immutable digest rather than rebuilt after testing.
- [ ] Dev deployment performs application-level smoke checks after rollout.
- [ ] Release checks become artifact-, compatibility-, install-, and upgrade-focused; any source-suite reduction happens only after artifact identity makes it provably safe.
- [ ] Static workflow contract tests fail closed if event filters, dependency chains, required check names, exact-candidate coverage, or publication safety drift.
- [ ] Expected and observed latency/reliability improvements are recorded after rollout.

## Evidence and related work

- PR #566 adopted scoped local verification and durable failure disposition.
- PR #602 moved the complete backend E2E suite from ordinary PRs to the exact merge candidate without weakening the shared-dev gate.
- Repository report: `docs/plans/2026-08-15-ci-reliability-and-latency.md`.

## Non-goals

- Weakening the full exact-candidate gate for the shared dev image.
- More sharding as the primary solution.
- Masking failures with retries, larger timeouts, quarantine, skip, or xfail.
- Changing branch protection, repository settings, production configuration, or release pinning as an immediate shortcut.

draft.title: [feature]: Add capability-aware Chat artifact generation
draft.body:
## Summary

Add capability-aware artifact generation to Chat V3. Known models should be classified from a maintained public catalog first, unknown or custom endpoints should be verified once in Settings, and models with tool calling should create files through isolated local tools rather than emitting binary document data themselves.

## Current state

- Chat accepts image, PDF, CSV, and text attachments, but model-tier configuration contains no capability metadata.
- Pydantic AI transports binary input but does not reliably discover input modality support for arbitrary compatible endpoints.
- Pydantic AI Harness is currently used for compaction and oversized tool-output handling, not artifact execution.
- Chat persists text and tool results only; there is no durable generated-artifact contract, stream event, SDK type, or output drawer.
- The Bifrost SDK can read and write files, but cannot promote workflow output into a conversation artifact.
- MCP workflow results are generally wrapped as text and structured JSON rather than standard media/resource content blocks.

## Proposed approach

### Model capabilities

- Resolve recognized model IDs through the OpenRouter Models API and cache:
  - input modalities
  - output modalities
  - tool and tool-choice support
  - structured-output support
- Use Pydantic model profiles only as secondary hints.
- Fall back conservatively for unknown models and custom IDs.
- Provide a one-time Settings conformance test for text, forced tool calling, image input, PDF input, and native image output.
- Persist the result with its source, timestamp, and a fingerprint of provider, endpoint, model, and declared capability configuration.
- Invalidate verification when the fingerprint changes.
- Keep model-native capabilities distinct from capabilities supplied by Bifrost tools.

### Artifact execution

- Do not ask the model to synthesize PDF, DOCX, XLSX, or image bytes.
- Expose artifact creation and isolated Python execution tools to tool-capable models.
- Give each run an isolated working directory with a dedicated output directory.
- Collect only declared output files and validate filename, size, MIME signature, and allowed format before storage.
- Store durable conversation artifacts with origin, status, MIME type, filename, size, message/tool/execution association, and storage key.
- Emit artifact-started, artifact-ready, and artifact-failed stream events.
- Support direct validated content artifacts such as text, Markdown, JSON, CSV, HTML, and SVG.
- Support binary artifacts created by the sandbox, custom workflows, or configured generation providers.

Before selecting implementations or dependencies, survey proven open-source document-generation projects and established libraries. Prefer maintained libraries and reusable patterns for PDF, XLSX, DOCX, charts, and images over custom file-format code. Record licensing and runtime constraints for anything adopted or used as prompt/instruction inspiration.

### Settings and Chat UI

- Show model-native capability controls and verification state alongside Fast, Balanced, and Pro.
- Separately show capabilities available through Bifrost tools.
- Gate attachment affordances and artifact tools against the effective selected tier.
- Render artifacts as inline cards that open a right-side output sheet.
- Show loading feedback immediately; hide PDF/image viewers until load and crossfade them in.
- Provide download, error, retry, empty, responsive, and reduced-motion states.

### SDK and workflows

- Extend `bifrost.ai.complete` and `bifrost.ai.stream` with file/artifact inputs and artifact outputs.
- Add typed artifact events to streaming responses.
- Add a typed `ArtifactRef` plus `bifrost.artifacts.create/read` for custom workflows.
- Allow a workflow tool to accept artifact references and return generated artifacts without base64 payloads.

### MCP interoperability

- Accept artifact inputs through authenticated artifact IDs or URIs in JSON tool arguments.
- Translate artifact outputs into MCP image, resource-link, or embedded-resource content blocks as appropriate.
- Publish output schemas and author documentation for custom workflow tools.
- Keep interactive MCP Apps and arbitrary `ui://` resource hosting out of this issue.

## Acceptance criteria

- A recognized model receives catalog-derived capability suggestions without a provider call.
- An unknown or custom-endpoint model can be tested in Settings and retains verified results until its fingerprint changes.
- DeepSeek V4 Pro is represented as text-only model input/output with tool calling available.
- Any verified tool-capable Chat tier can create supported artifacts through Bifrost tools even when the model has no native binary output.
- A custom workflow can accept an artifact reference, generate a PDF or other file, return an artifact reference, and have Chat persist, preview, and download it.
- The output drawer presents immediate progress instead of a blank PDF frame.
- Bifrost MCP returns standards-compliant file/media result blocks for artifact-producing workflows.
- SDK and custom-workflow documentation includes complete input/output examples.
- Backend unit and E2E tests, SDK tests, React component tests, and one Playwright happy path cover the feature.

## Out of scope

- Rendering arbitrary MCP Apps or hosting third-party `ui://` interfaces.
- Treating public model catalogs as authoritative for unknown custom endpoints.
- Running model-generated code directly inside the API or trusted workflow process.

draft.title: [feature]: Make scheduler jobs observable and memory admission adaptive
draft.body:
## Summary

Scheduler Diagnostics reports aggregate queue and memory-wait counts, but omits on-demand platform jobs such as Solution deploys. Memory admission also applies one fixed 768 MiB headroom requirement to every Solution deploy, including locally prebuilt bundles that do not run npm or Vite on the server.

## Current behavior

- Queued on-demand jobs are visible only as aggregate counts.
- Running jobs appear only as bare UUIDs under scheduler replicas.
- The System schedules table contains recurring task definitions, so on-demand jobs never appear there.
- Solution deploy admission uses a static job-type requirement rather than the actual build path or observed workload.
- The UI does not show available versus required headroom.

## Expected behavior

- Scheduler Diagnostics has a distinct Platform jobs section for queued, memory-blocked, running, waiting, and cancellation-requested work.
- Operators can see job title, type, resource, requester, phase/progress, age/runtime, attempts, errors, and available actions.
- Memory waits explain available and required headroom.
- Prebuilt deploys are distinguished from server-side builds.
- Unknown builds use a safe cold-start floor, while later builds use environment-aware observed peaks keyed by app/build fingerprint with safety margin.
- Hard memory enforcement remains in place when an estimate underpredicts usage.

## Acceptance criteria

- Backend contracts expose the admission details needed by the shared PlatformJob status surface.
- Scheduler Diagnostics consumes the shared platform-job list instead of inventing a feature-specific queue.
- Per-build telemetry is attributable and invalidated when source, dependencies, or toolchain identity changes.
- Multi-app deploy accounting handles sequential build transients and retained compiled output.
- Backend unit/E2E, React component, and one administrator Playwright happy-path test cover the change.
- Existing scheduled-task diagnostics remain distinct and functional.

## Production evidence

Recent one-app Solution deploys increased scheduler working set by roughly 240-330 MiB and peaked around 487-574 MiB. A deploy waited under a 1 GiB pod limit because only about 749 MiB was available against the fixed 768 MiB rule, then completed after baseline memory fell, peaking near 418 MiB.

- **OpenAI API key** for usage-based API billing

- [ ] AI Provider Configuration UI

- [ ] Provider configuration create and update endpoints
- [ ] `/api/sdk/ai/complete`
- [ ] Workflow execution and usage reporting

### 1. Sign in with ChatGPT

Support the browser or device-code authentication flow provided by Codex.

This mode should use the customer’s eligible ChatGPT subscription instead of OpenAI API billing.

### 2. Codex access token

Support Codex access tokens for trusted, unattended Bifrost installations where the ChatGPT workspace permits their use.

This would be suitable for private workflow runners and scheduled jobs.

### 3. OpenAI API key

Retain API-key authentication for customers who prefer usage-based OpenAI Platform billing.

The UI should clearly distinguish API billing from ChatGPT subscription access.

## Functional requirements

- [ ] Show Codex as a selectable provider

- OpenAI API-key billing

- A different model with separate billing

If Codex subscription authentication is unavailable, the workflow should fail with a clear error.

Any provider or billing-mode change should require an explicit administrator action.

## Security requirements

- [ ] Encrypt access and refresh tokens at rest
- [ ] Never expose credentials through browser code

- [ ] Never write credentials to workflow or application logs
- [ ] Do not require users to manually copy `auth.json`

draft.title: [bug]: Event subscription filter_expression is persisted but never enforced
draft.body:
### Summary

Event subscriptions accept, persist, export, import, and advertise an optional JSONPath `filter_expression`, but event processing never evaluates it. A subscription with a non-matching filter still queues its workflow or agent target.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create a webhook or topic event source.
2. Subscribe a workflow with the matching event type and `filter_expression: "$.priority == 'high'"`.
3. Emit an otherwise matching event whose payload contains `priority: "low"`.
4. Inspect the event deliveries and workflow executions.

### Expected behavior

The subscription filter is evaluated before target dispatch. A non-matching event does not queue the target. Invalid or unevaluable filters fail closed and leave an observable decision instead of silently running automation.

### Actual behavior

Both `EventProcessor.emit_topic()` and `EventProcessor._process_delivery()` select active subscriptions by source and event type, then create pending deliveries without reading `subscription.filter_expression`. `queue_event_deliveries()` consequently queues the target.

This is especially surprising because the field is exposed through the REST contracts, CLI, manifest round-trip, and Solution deployment, and is described as a JSONPath expression. Some contract text calls it "future use", but no mutation surface rejects it or warns that it is inert.

### Environment

`gobifrost/bifrost` `main` at `7fbda650359c9bdbacb0b4cc373cd4c3b3ff6ff3`.

### Logs / screenshots

No exception is emitted. Code inspection shows neither delivery-creation path evaluates `filter_expression`; a linked draft PR will add regression coverage and a proposed fail-closed implementation.

draft.title: [bug]: Preserve terminal 429 errors and make AI retries resilient to request bursts
draft.body:
## Summary

Production agent runs that exhaust OpenRouter rate-limit retries are incorrectly recorded as `Connection error`. The shared retry transport is active, but a concurrent ticket burst caused all three attempts to complete within roughly one second, after which an underlying `httpx2.HTTPStatusError: 429 Too Many Requests` was translated through the OpenAI/Pydantic adapter into a generic connection failure.

This makes the incident look like networking trouble, prevents operators and recovery logic from distinguishing rate limiting, and leaves ordinary burst traffic insufficient time to recover.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure an agent model through OpenRouter using the shared retry transport introduced by #648.
2. Return HTTP 429 without a useful `Retry-After` header for all three transport attempts, or generate enough concurrent agent work to trigger that condition.
3. Observe two rapid `ai_provider_request_retry` warnings followed by terminal failure.
4. Inspect the exception chain and persisted AgentRun error.

Production evidence from 2026-08-27:

- `f9afca55-8657-4883-938d-98eb166a26c0`
- `230e161c-3e8a-4909-aa54-d5f576c98460`
- `e3b8b693-1141-4db5-befb-1186dbf1cede`
- `3bb91120-936b-4e84-804b-f0ca7020dbbb`
- `66b72771-9a76-457b-a2db-b95911e98c84`
- `f59b1fdb-48e7-427d-b767-232486a52841`
- `264843f2-0d96-43da-ac40-cc2de718a558`

All seven visible production traces contain an underlying 429. Several occurred during a simultaneous monitoring-alert burst across worker pods.

## Expected behavior

- A terminal 429 remains identifiable as a rate-limit failure throughout the transport, Pydantic/OpenAI adapter, AgentRun, and operator-facing diagnostics.
- Bounded retry behavior spans a meaningful provider recovery window when `Retry-After` is absent, while remaining jittered and finite.
- Concurrent workers do not synchronize rapid retries into the same rate-limit window.
- The selected provider remains authoritative; no silent provider fallback is introduced.
- Retry and terminal logs expose privacy-safe provider, model, surface, attempt count, delay, status code, and root error type.
- Tests cover successful recovery after a temporary 429, exhausted 429 classification, and concurrent burst behavior.

## Actual behavior

- `MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3` with a short random-exponential fallback can exhaust in approximately one second.
- The retry transport raises `httpx2.HTTPStatusError` after exhaustion.
- The OpenAI client wraps that exception as `openai.APIConnectionError`.
- Pydantic AI then persists `ModelAPIError: Connection error`, hiding the actual 429.
- Halo ticket recovery eventually returns abandoned tickets, but completed delegated work can be lost before the parent updates Halo.

## Environment

- Production image: `ghcr.io/gobifrost/bifrost-api:1.2.1-dev.58`
- Retry implementation: #648 / commit `f1270817`
- Provider: OpenRouter
- Observed model: `google/gemini-3.7-flash`
- Relevant code:
  - `api/src/services/agent_runtime/retry_transport.py`
  - `api/src/services/agent_runtime/model_factory.py`
  - `api/src/services/agent_runtime/observed_model.py`
  - `api/src/services/execution/autonomous_agent_executor.py`

## Notes

The smallest safe fix should preserve the existing no-provider-fallback and bounded-retry policy. It should correct terminal exception translation and make the fallback delay useful under a real burst, rather than adding an independent outer retry loop.

draft.title: [enhancement]: Define safe 429 recovery for raw AI media and discovery calls
draft.body:
## Context

#656 makes model requests and embeddings use one bounded, burst-resilient retry transport while preserving terminal HTTP status identity. The runtime audit found remaining direct AI-provider HTTP surfaces that do not share that contract:

- image/video upload and generation POSTs;
- OpenRouter media catalog and pricing/discovery GETs;
- some direct surfaces still flatten provider failures into generic errors.

Blindly replaying a media POST is unsafe because the provider may have accepted it before the client observed a timeout/429, potentially duplicating jobs or charges. Read-only catalog/discovery GETs have a different idempotency profile and can generally use bounded retry.

## Desired behavior

Every AI-provider surface has an explicit, tested 429 contract. Safe/idempotent reads reuse bounded jittered retry. Potentially accepted writes use provider-supported idempotency keys, operation IDs/status recovery, or remain terminal with an actionable structured error—never an unexamined automatic replay.

## Acceptance criteria

1. Inventory every direct AI-provider HTTP surface and classify it as idempotent read, idempotent write, recoverable async submission, or unsafe-to-replay write.
2. Preserve provider/status/root error identity through the public and operator-facing error surfaces.
3. Apply the shared bounded retry policy to safe reads, including missing/invalid/non-positive `Retry-After` behavior.
4. For image/video submissions, use documented provider idempotency or operation recovery when available; otherwise do not replay and explain why.
5. Add tests for temporary recovery, exhausted 429 classification, concurrent bursts, timeout-after-possible-acceptance, and no duplicate submission.
6. Log privacy-safe provider, model/surface, attempt, delay, status, and operation/idempotency identity.
7. Do not introduce silent provider fallback.

draft.title: [bug]: Keep workflow history ordering and live pagination consistent

## Summary

Production History mixes a stale cancelled scheduled execution into the newest page because backend ordering uses nullable `started_at`, while the UI groups by `started_at ?? scheduled_at`. Live WebSocket inserts also grow the first-page cache without updating its cursor.

- Backend ordering and keyset cursor use the same effective timeline timestamp.
- Scheduled, cancelled, pending, and completed rows paginate deterministically.

draft.title: [feature]: Add policy-controlled retries for execution-engine failures
draft.body:
## Problem

A workflow execution can remain `running` after its worker or execution subprocess disappears. Age-based cleanup cannot tell a slow execution from one whose owner is gone.

Bifrost already has durable execution records and retry machinery, but it has no workflow-level policy for retrying eligible execution-engine failures. Operators must fail these executions or restart them by hand.

This work is separate from the scheduler-owned platform jobs in #532. It applies to user workflows running on execution workers.

## Proposed solution

Add policy-controlled infrastructure retries to registered workflows. The default remains off.

When a retryable engine failure occurs, Bifrost may start a new attempt for the same logical execution. The new attempt uses the code, inputs, and resolved retry policy captured when the execution was dispatched.

Eligible failures could include worker loss and execution-subprocess crashes. User-code exceptions, cancellation, configuration errors, and timeouts should not retry by default.

The worker should hold a renewable lease while it owns an attempt. Each worker process needs an incarnation ID so a replacement process cannot inherit the old process's ownership by reusing its worker or pod name. After the lease expires, Bifrost fences the old attempt before creating another one. Late progress or completion writes from the old attempt must fail.

Bifrost does not capture Python runtime state. A retry starts at the workflow entry point. Workflow authors remain responsible for replay safety through idempotency, durable cursors, or other domain-specific commit rules.

The retry policy belongs on the registered Workflow and must flow through API contracts, UI, CLI, MCP, manifests, Solutions, and execution history. Bifrost should copy the resolved policy onto each execution at dispatch so later workflow edits cannot change an active run.

A policy might contain:

```yaml
execution_retry:
  enabled: true
  max_attempts: 2
  retry_on:
    - worker_lost
    - subprocess_crash
```

The exact contract should reuse the existing retry path where possible.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Retry policy is stored on Workflow and defaults to disabled.
- [ ] API, UI, CLI, MCP, manifests, and Solutions expose the policy.
- [ ] Dispatch copies the resolved policy, pinned code, and inputs onto the execution.
- [ ] Each attempt records its worker identity and worker incarnation ID.
- [ ] Workers renew bounded leases for active attempts.
- [ ] Lease expiry fences the old attempt before another attempt starts.
- [ ] A fenced attempt cannot publish progress or terminal state.
- [ ] Eligible infrastructure failures create a new attempt under the same logical execution ID.
- [ ] The old attempt records a specific terminal status such as `worker_lost`.
- [ ] Attempt limits apply across the whole logical execution.
- [ ] User-code exceptions, cancellation, and configuration failures do not retry automatically.
- [ ] Tests cover owner loss, subprocess crashes, a same-name worker with a new incarnation, late writes from fenced attempts, concurrent cleanup, and attempt exhaustion.
- [ ] A chaos test kills the owner between two durable side effects and proves that an application cursor can avoid repeating the completed side effect.

## Production evidence

We tested the mechanism downstream with a Meraki configuration-delta backup workflow. The first attempt committed one organization, then we deleted its exact owner pod. Bifrost marked that attempt `worker_lost`. A second attempt started on a different worker incarnation and completed the workflow. The workflow's own cursor skipped the organization already committed.

The work queue drained, poison-queue counts stayed unchanged, temporary autoscaling controls were restored, and health checks passed before and after the test.

Reference implementation:

- https://github.com/Midtown-Technology-Group/bifrost/pull/642
- https://github.com/Midtown-Technology-Group/bifrost/pull/643

The downstream patch only implements and tests the recovery mechanism. It does not add the full workflow policy or carry it through every product contract.

## Design doc link

None yet. This issue is meant to settle the contract before an implementation PR.

draft.title: [feature]: add claim-backed path containment to file policies
draft.body:
## Problem

File policies can resolve custom claims, but the existing `in` operator only compares an exact file path with an exact claim value. Hierarchical resource grants therefore require one policy row per literal path prefix. A document-management solution with independent site, document-category, and view/download grants grows as sites × categories × access modes and must regenerate policies whenever a scope is added.

Table policies have a related but distinct modeling constraint: independent claims for two dimensions create an unsafe Cartesian product. Composite grant keys and flattened grant rows are the correct table representation. A scale spike also showed that compiling hundreds of path prefixes into SQL is over 1,000× slower than an exact composite-key `IN` query, so path containment should not be added to table expressions.

## Proposed solution

Add a file-policy-only, segment-aware `path_within_any` predicate, inspired by OPA `strings.any_prefix_match` and XACML `any-of(string-starts-with)`. It accepts a scalar file path and a list or claim-resolved list of permitted path scopes, returning true only when the path equals a non-empty scope or is its slash-delimited descendant.

Keep this as an ABAC predicate over existing server-resolved claims. Do not introduce glob or raw `startswith` semantics. Table policies continue to use exact composite access keys with the existing `in` operator. Flattening list-valued claim sources is separate follow-up work.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `path_within_any` is accepted by `FileExpr` and rejected by generic/table `Expr`.
- [ ] It accepts exactly `[path, literal-list-or-claims-reference]`.
- [ ] Exact paths and slash-delimited descendants match.
- [ ] Sibling prefixes such as `site-a` and `site-annex` do not match.
- [ ] Missing, empty, malformed, and non-string claim values fail closed; an empty/root claim cannot grant the whole resource hierarchy.
- [ ] One root file policy is proven against a synthetic site × document-category × PDF/download grant matrix.
- [ ] Table access is proven with a composite site/category key and the existing exact `in` operator.
- [ ] A large synthetic benchmark seeds 150 sites, 8 categories, 60,000 documents, 120,000 file-metadata records, and sparse/medium/broad permission sets up to 320 composite grants and 480 file scopes per user.
- [ ] Benchmark evidence includes seed time, policy evaluation throughput, end-to-end sampled file authorization, SQL `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`, query time, and memory where measurable.
- [ ] The benchmark compares one root claim-backed file policy against 2,400 generated literal-prefix policy rows and records the rejected SQL path-containment experiment.
- [ ] Correctness tests cover sibling-prefix isolation and view-only/download denial within the large fixture without machine-specific timing assertions in CI.
- [ ] Targeted policy, claims, file-service, and live storage-boundary tests pass.

## Design doc link (optional)

N/A — implementation spike will document the decision and evidence in the PR.

draft.title: [bug]: Preserve valid chat chunks and hide internal execution errors
draft.body:
## Summary

Durable Chat serializes valid `ChatStreamChunk` models with `exclude_none=True`, which removes required-but-null fields such as `ToolResult.result`. The Redis publisher then revalidates the malformed dictionary, causing a secondary Pydantic failure. The terminal error path publishes `str(exception)` and the client renders it verbatim, exposing internal validation details to users.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Run an agent tool from Chat that returns a normal tool error with `result=None`.
2. The agent executor produces a valid `ChatStreamChunk(type="tool_result", ...)`.
3. The durable Chat consumer serializes it with `exclude_none=True`, removing the required `result` key.
4. `publish_chat_run_event` revalidates the payload and raises a Pydantic missing-field error.
5. Chat publishes and displays that raw exception instead of a safe user-facing failure.

## Expected behavior

- Every valid `ChatStreamChunk` remains valid after serialization and replay.
- Required null fields are preserved while irrelevant unset fields may remain omitted.
- Expected domain errors remain actionable.
- Internal exceptions remain available in logs and admin run diagnostics but never travel through the user-facing Chat stream.

## Actual behavior

A normal failed tool result can fail Chat event publication, terminate the run, and expose raw Pydantic details in the Chat UI.

## Acceptance criteria

- Centralize contract-safe Chat chunk serialization.
- Replace all direct `exclude_none=True` Chat-event serialization call sites.
- Preserve full diagnostic exceptions in the run record and logs.
- Publish only safe public terminal errors to Chat.
- Add backend round-trip coverage for all Chat chunk variants, including failed tools and successful tools returning null.
- Add client defense-in-depth coverage preventing internal error details from rendering inline.

## Notes

The delegated/shared-mailbox state-token defect discovered during the incident is separate and intentionally out of scope for this issue.

draft.title: Enforce workspace-module cache refresh at the shared execution boundary
draft.body:
### Problem

simple_worker clears stale virtual workspace modules before delegating to worker._run_execution, but the shared _run_execution function does not enforce that invariant itself.

That makes cache correctness dependent on every caller remembering the preflight step. Any direct caller, alternate worker path, or test harness that invokes _run_execution can reuse workspace dependencies already present in sys.modules. If an entry module has refreshed while one of its imported helpers has not, a single execution can observe mixed module generations.

We encountered this in a downstream deployment with release-aware execution routing: a newly deployed workflow called a new helper signature, but the process retained the prior helper module and failed with an unexpected-keyword error. Restarting or renaming/versioning the module would mask the issue; neither establishes a reliable execution invariant.

### Suggested invariant

The shared execution boundary should own workspace-module refresh/eviction after activating the execution context and before importing workspace code. If refresh fails, temporary solution/workspace/generation context should also be cleared before the exception escapes.

simple_worker can retain its earlier preflight if it is required for imports that happen before _run_execution, but correctness of _run_execution itself should not depend on that caller-specific behavior.

### Why this may matter upstream

The exact downstream trigger involved release-aware routing that is not present upstream, so I am not claiming the same production symptom is currently reproducible in stock Bifrost. The architectural gap is present upstream, however: simple_worker performs the refresh and then calls a shared function that does not independently enforce it.

We have a small defensive patch and focused regression tests downstream and would be happy to contribute a scoped PR if maintainers agree that _run_execution is the right invariant boundary.

draft.title: [bug]: Remove request-path full GC and bound large table-response memory
draft.body:
## Summary

Large table-document requests synchronously invoke `gc.collect()` and `malloc_trim()` on the API event loop, causing multi-second stalls, failed health checks, and pod restarts. Build a production-shaped memory regression harness, remove request-path full GC, and audit the Ninja site-health workflow for persisted-data and response amplification.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Run an API replica with the current `AllocationTrimMiddleware`.
2. Repeatedly request production-shaped table pages of approximately 500 documents and 230–400 KiB.
3. Continuously probe `/health` while sampling request latency, RSS, cgroup memory, explicit GC, and allocator trimming.
4. Compare current behavior with normal Python teardown and, if justified, allocator trimming without full GC.

Production evidence:

- A 20-second `py-spy` capture sampled `gc.collect()` at `allocation_trim.py:55` 822 times.
- `/health` stopped advancing during collections.
- Direct PostgreSQL selection takes roughly 50–60 ms and JSON/Pydantic parsing roughly 20 ms.
- Equivalent API requests have taken 38–101 seconds.
- Restarting the API temporarily restores performance.
- Existing tests assert only that GC and trimming functions were called.

## Expected behavior

- No synchronous full GC on the API request/event-loop path.
- Large responses complete without multi-second GC pauses.
- `/health` remains responsive under repeated large-response load.
- Settled memory does not grow monotonically between benchmark rounds.
- Existing protections such as `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2`, bounded parsing, and targeted allocator trimming for proven exceptional bursts remain intact.
- Ninja state and workflow results contain only data with demonstrated consumers.

## Actual behavior

Every qualifying table-document request or response of at least 64 KiB triggers process-wide full GC and allocator trimming. The stop-the-world collections block unrelated traffic and health checks. The middleware has no RSS/latency evidence demonstrating that it prevents the original OOM condition.

The Ninja site-health workflow may separately amplify requests, persisted state, writes, or stored execution results; its exact live behavior requires read-only inspection.

## Environment

- Production: `https://bifrost.gocovi.com`
- Kubernetes: `do-nyc1-gocovi-apps`, namespace `bifrost`
- Two API replicas, one Uvicorn process each
- Relevant commits: `d3fcc69c6`, `dccd6f0e3`, PR #621
- Ninja workflow: `workflows/ninja_site_tracker.py`
- Fingerprint workflow: `e460dcf2-9fd5-4609-893d-00dc05f4d7c8`
- Scan workflow: `6f633da5-6a5c-48dc-97e7-706e74306e75`
- State table: `ninja_device_site_state` (`18dc9f81-d141-4341-8b23-30c166ec4d03`)
- Observed source version: `sha256:1191c1e9a2cb7efa798fa949c5d56c470f29484895aa47ded93dc39dd3e444a0`

## Scope and acceptance

- Add a deterministic large-table-response benchmark measuring request and health latency, peak/settled RSS, cgroup indicators, retained growth, and explicit GC/trim time.
- Distinguish live references, collectible cycles, reusable allocator pages, and genuine monotonic growth.
- Replace call-count-only middleware tests with stall, latency, and retained-memory regressions.
- Produce a measured Ninja field inventory and guarded, undeployed workflow revision.
- Prefer bounded bulk operations over per-device writes.
- Return compact scan summaries rather than full device/state collections.
- Keep Sales Hunter analysis separate and propose follow-up work only if it materially affects reproduction.
- Make no production deployment or live workflow mutation without explicit approval.

draft.title: [feature]: Accept base64-encoded webhook HMAC signatures
draft.body:
### Problem

Incoming webhook HMAC verification only accepts hex-encoded signatures. Senders that base64-encode the same HMAC-SHA256 digest are rejected as invalid, even when the shared secret is correct. Base64 is a common convention across PSA/RMM and cloud event vendors.

Related: HaloPSA sends a space between the prefix and the digest (sha256= <sig>), which also fails verification because the prefix is stripped by length without trimming.

The result is that users with a correctly configured secret see signature failures they can’t diagnose or work around.

### Proposed solution

Accept either canonical encoding of the same HMAC-SHA256 digest — hex or base64 — and tolerate whitespace around the prefix and header value. Verification stays constant-time, and existing hex behaviour is unchanged.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Base64 signatures verify successfully, with or without a configured prefix
- [ ] HaloPSA’s sha256= <sig> form (space after the prefix) verifies successfully
- [ ] Tampered or malformed signatures are still rejected
- [ ] Existing hex signature behaviour is unchanged
- [ ] The public SDK webhook helper behaves identically to the runtime verifier
- [ ] Unit and endpoint-level test coverage for the new formats

### Design doc link (optional)

_No response_

draft.title: [bug]: Preserve workflow completion when Redis execution tracking expires
draft.body:
## Summary
Long-running workflows can outlive their temporary Redis execution record. The worker then completes successfully but cannot record the terminal result, leaving PostgreSQL execution history stuck at Running.

## Expected behavior
A running worker must retain recoverable execution state for its entire lifetime, and completion must reconcile against PostgreSQL if Redis tracking is missing.

## Actual behavior
After the Redis record expires, the completion consumer logs “No pending record found for result” and skips the terminal transition.

## Proposed fix
Maintain a compact parent-owned Redis execution lease, refresh or recreate it in batched intervals, retain PostgreSQL as the source of truth, and recover terminal processing from PostgreSQL when Redis state is absent.

draft.title: [bug]: make document-prefix pagination use selective indexes
draft.body:
## Summary
Prefix-and-cursor document queries can choose `Limit → Gather Merge → Sort → Parallel Seq Scan` under `en_US.UTF-8`, causing every page to scan unrelated documents.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Populate the shared `documents` relation with millions of documents across multiple tables and tenant-style ID prefixes under `en_US.UTF-8`.
2. Call `tables.query(document_id_prefix=..., after_document_id=..., skip_count=True, limit=500)`.

## Expected behavior
Prefix-and-cursor pages use selective indexed work whose cost does not grow with unrelated tenants' documents. Literal prefixes preserve `%`, `_`, escape-character, and Unicode semantics. Pagination remains stable and policy/table isolation remains intact.

## Actual behavior
The current locale-aware lower bound plus `LIKE` predicate has no selective upper index bound. PostgreSQL can scan and sort the shared relation for every page despite the cursor and limit.

## Environment
- Production PostgreSQL collation: `en_US.UTF-8`
- Existing indexes: primary key `(table_id, id)`, btree `(table_id)`, GIN `(data)`
- Implementation: `api/src/routers/tables.py`

- RCA: `sharepoint-explorer/docs/performance/2026-09-12-reporting-rca.md`
- Plan artifact: `sharepoint-explorer/docs/performance/2026-09-12-report-query-plans.json`
- Observed production plan: `Limit → Gather Merge → Sort → Parallel Seq Scan`
- Bounded read-only UUID-specific experiment: 500 rows in 26 ms using `documents_pkey`; this is evidence only, not a generic fix.

- Existing released SDK callers remain compatible.

- Replacement and merge semantics are explicit and tested.
- No duplicate route or dead implementation remains.

draft.title: [feature]: Detect and persist Anthropic prompt-cache support

## Summary

## Proposed behavior

- Store a tri-state capability on each AI provider connection: `unknown`, `supported`, or `unsupported`.
- For an unknown Anthropic endpoint, attempt the request with prompt caching enabled.

- Concurrent first requests cannot corrupt capability state or cause unsafe retry behavior.

- Migration, DTO/contract, service, and request-path tests cover all three states and the exact fallback classification.
- Focused and full pre-PR verification pass.

draft.title: [feature]: Spike Kubernetes-aware elastic execution control plane
draft.body:
## Problem

Bifrost schedulers and workers currently combine work discovery with compute capacity. This preserves excellent warm-path workflow latency, but requires operators to provision enough always-on memory for peak workloads. Heavy PlatformJobs can threaten scheduler stability, fixed worker fleets remain allocated while idle, and small executions inherit substantially more runtime overhead than their work requires.

## Proposed solution

Design and spike an optional Bifrost Elastic Runtime for Kubernetes. Work is classified into a small set of execution lanes; existing warm executors consume eligible RabbitMQ lanes without an additional dispatch hop; KEDA supplies additional worker replicas or one-shot Job pods when queues have pressure. PostgreSQL remains authoritative for durable work and policy, Redis distributes policy-change notifications, and Kubernetes-native capacity is reconciled by the existing scheduler/control role rather than a new Bifrost orchestrator image.

The spike must preserve unchanged Docker behavior, keep the interactive workflow path fast, safely transition lane ownership through versioned policy, and investigate a slim one-shot execution path so resource requests reflect measured workload needs instead of the current full worker baseline.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Existing installations retain their current scheduler and worker behavior without enabling Elastic Runtime.
- [ ] API-triggered workflows retain their direct API → RabbitMQ → warm-worker path with no orchestrator hop.
- [ ] A small, stable set of lanes separates interactive, background, high-memory, and isolated work.
- [ ] Executor-pool subscriptions and warm minimums are controlled by versioned Bifrost policy.
- [ ] Local-to-elastic and elastic-to-local transitions provision capacity before draining old subscriptions.
- [ ] KEDA scales an existing worker Deployment from zero and from a configured warm minimum in a local Kind cluster.
- [ ] One heavy PlatformJob runs in a resource-limited, disposable Kubernetes Job pod.
- [ ] Scheduled-trigger leadership remains available through one lightweight control scheduler.
- [ ] Cancellation, controller restart, duplicate delivery, OOM, and unavailable node capacity have defined and tested behavior.
- [ ] Worker and one-shot runner baseline memory, incremental execution memory, image-pull time, cold-start time, and warm-path latency are measured.
- [ ] The design defines right-sized resource classes and investigates removing the full worker supervisor/template/pool overhead from one-shot execution.
- [ ] The spike concludes with a documented go/no-go recommendation and migration path toward a shared internal work/attempt contract.
- [ ] Docker compatibility and the existing public PlatformJob, workflow, and agent contracts remain intact.

## Design doc link (optional)

docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-15-kubernetes-elastic-runtime-design.md
