draft.title: [feature]: Per-profile AI model failover for transport-terminal provider errors
draft.body:
## Summary
Add an operator-configured failover pointer on AI model profiles so transport-terminal provider errors (429/5xx/connection errors after the 6-attempt/60s transport budget) roll over to another model/provider instead of failing the run.

## Motivation
Production agent-run analysis (90d: 6,351 completed / 90 failed, ~1.3%): failures cluster in upstream bursts — Jul 8–14 OpenRouter shared-pool 429s on deepseek-v4-flash, Aug 26–27 connection-error burst on gemini-3.7-flash — all after retries were exhausted. Failover rescues exactly this slice (~0.5–1% of runs, bursty). Token-limit, queue-timeout, validation, and tool-budget failures are out of scope for failover (deterministic or non-model).

## Approach
- `AIModelProfile.failover_profile_id` (nullable self-FK, RESTRICT, cycle + max-3-chain validation)
- `resolve_chain` skips unresolvable members (`ai_model_chain_skip`) and raises the head error when nothing resolves
- Per-request `FailoverModel` (sticky within a run; eligible = 408/429/5xx + SDK connection/timeout only; streams fail over on establishment only, never replayed)
- `failover_path` recorded in run metadata (JSON string) + `ai_model_failover` log + AIUsage per actually-serving model
- Admin UI fallback picker with same-connection warning; no-fallback policy amended to an allowlisted chain
- Different-connection fallback recommended for real quota isolation (same key = same shared pool)

## Verification
- Unit: classifier, wrapper (request/stream/sticky/settings), service lifecycle (validation, chain, delete guard, merge successor semantics, migration round-trip)
- HTTP e2e for the pointer round-trip, guards, and response shape
- Client vitest for the picker; Playwright AI-model-settings spec
- Live debug-stack verification against real cheap OpenRouter models: dead-endpoint primary (resolve skip), stub-500 primary (request-time switch with recorded path), 404 negative control failing fast without consuming fallback

## Follow-ups (not this issue)
- BYOK provider keys to leave the OpenRouter shared pool (the provider's own remedy hint in the 429 bodies)
- Worker capacity behind the 2100s queue timeouts
- 4000-cap agent overrides (Dispatch, Spam, Teams Concierge, Triage) as length-truncation candidates

draft.title: [bug]: Table update policies gate only pre-image, allows org-hop via mutation
draft.body:
## Summary
Table row `update` policy checks run against the pre-image (`old_row`) only. A user authorized to write a row (e.g. `row.organization_id == user.organization_id` matches their own org) can mutate the row into a value they should not be able to write — e.g. retarget `organization_id` to another org. The write succeeds because the post-image (target value) is never policy-checked.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Global table with `own_org_full` policy on read/create/update/delete: `when: {eq: [{row: organization_id}, {user: organization_id}]}` (+ admin_bypass).
2. Alice (org1) inserts her own row with `organization_id = org1` — succeeds (correct).
3. Alice PATCHes her own row with `{"organization_id": "<org2_id>"}` — currently succeeds (BUG), should be 403.
4. Same hole on upsert paths (`POST documents` with `upsert=true`, `POST documents/upsert`) and batch upsert (`merge_upsert` / `replace_upsert`), which check `update` on the old row only.

## Expected behavior
Mutation policies are evaluated against both the existing record and the target value:
- Update (PATCH merge, single upsert-update, batch upsert-update): require `update` on BOTH pre-image and post-image (merged for PATCH/merge_upsert, replaced for replace_upsert/single upsert). Deny if either fails.
- Insert (no existing row): `create` on the candidate row (unchanged).
- Delete: `delete` on the pre-image (unchanged).
- Single `POST documents/upsert` against an existing id is an update: gate on `update` (both images), not `create`.

## Actual behavior
`api/src/routers/tables.py::update_document`, `insert_document` (upsert branch), and `upsert_document` call `_check_action_or_403("update", ..., old_row, ...)` and never check the post-image. `api/shared/table_batch_writes.py::_check_policies` checks `update` on `old_row` only (`continue` skips any target check).

`api/tests/e2e/platform/test_policies.py::test_update_gates_on_pre_image_only` explicitly pins the pre-image-only behavior and must be updated to the new dual-gate semantics.

## Notes
- Files: `api/src/routers/tables.py` (insert/upsert/update branches), `api/shared/table_batch_writes.py` (`_check_policies` + post-image construction per mode), e2e coverage in `api/tests/e2e/platform/test_policies.py`.
- Out of scope but noted: MCP table tools (`api/src/services/mcp_server/tools/tables.py`) do no policy evaluation at all (existing MCP-vs-REST drift).

draft.title: [bug]: Agent workflow execution loses identity needed for role checks
draft.body:
## Summary
Agent workflow execution loses the trusted executing agent identity needed for role checks.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Configure a specialist agent with a role required by a protected workflow tool.
2. Trigger it from an autonomous workflow using the intentionally roleless system account.
3. Invoke a tool that validates explicit role membership through its execution context.

## Expected behavior
The tool can evaluate the configured executing agent role through a trusted platform-provided identity, independently of requester/customer authorization. Human caller identity stays available for audit and separate checks.

AgentWorkflowCaller carries the initiating user but no agent identifier. execute_tool/ExecutionContext retain only is_agent=true. ## Environment

## Notes
Carry the actual executing agent through the canonical tool boundary and queue/worker context; expose a supported agent-aware explicit-role check using existing role permissions paths. Preserve human checks, deny missing/forged identity, and prevent delegated children from inheriting parent roles. Regression coverage must include queue rehydration and protected-tool invocation, without external customer mutations.

draft.title: [bug]: bifrost files search silently misses most files; indexing has four policies and the reconciler resurrects deletes
draft.body:
## Summary
`bifrost files search` (CLI / SDK / MCP / editor) silently misses most matching files, and the source index behind it is written by several code paths with different rules.

## Steps to reproduce / evidence
- Search scans at most 500 `file_index` rows with no `ORDER BY`, *then* matches in Python. On production (2,360 files) searching `halo` returned hits from 176 of 1,026 matching files with `truncated: false`.
- Glob → SQL `LIKE` translation is wrong: `workflows/*.py` matches nested files, `**/foo.py` misses a root `foo.py`, `_` acts as a wildcard, `*.{py,json}` matches nothing.
- Four indexing policies: editor/CLI writes index everything (binary as `""`), git sync / bundle import use an extension allowlist (no `.json`, `.ps1`, extensionless), the reconciler has no size cap, signed uploads leave `content=NULL` forever.
- `ref_rewriter`, app auto-migration, folder markers and `requirements.txt` saves write `_repo/` without touching the index → stale search results.
- The `workspace.file_index_reconcile` platform job never compares hashes (296 prod runs since Aug 7 all reported zero changes) and **writes deleted files back to S3** from the index ("reverse-sync").
- Solution install source (`_solutions/{id}/`, 886 files in prod) is not indexed at all.
- MCP `search_content` is a second, divergent implementation that loads every row per call.

## Expected behavior
One indexer and one search system. Small default pages (25) with a cursor and a plain-language next step an AI can act on. Search covers workspace **and** Solution source (Solution hits labelled read-only), with correct ripgrep-style globs.

## Notes
Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-01-unified-file-search.md`

draft.title: [bug]: bifrost login device flow fails with HTTP 429 after ~55s without approval
draft.body:
### Summary

The browser device-code login exits with `Error polling for token: 429` if the user takes longer than about 55 seconds to approve. The token endpoint's rate limit is lower than the polling rate the server itself advertises.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run `bifrost login` (device-code flow) against any instance with rate limiting active (non-testing environment).
2. Wait about a minute before approving in the browser.

### Expected behavior

The CLI keeps waiting until the user approves or the device code expires (`expires_in`, 300s).

### Actual behavior

The 11th poll returns HTTP 429 and the CLI prints `Error polling for token: 429` and exits.

### Environment

- `main` (also seen on a 1.4.2-dev CLI build)

### Logs / screenshots

Cause:

- `POST /auth/device/code` returns `interval: 5`, so the CLI polls about 12 times per minute.
- `POST /auth/device/token` is guarded by `auth_limiter.check("device_token", client_ip)` in `api/src/routers/auth.py`, and `auth_limiter = RateLimiter(max_requests=10, window_seconds=60)` (`api/src/core/rate_limit.py`). The endpoint's docstring says "Rate limited: 20 requests per minute per IP address (allows polling)", but the shared 10/min limiter is used.
- `login_flow` in `api/bifrost/cli.py` treats any non-200 poll response as fatal, so a 429 (or an RFC 8628 `slow_down`) ends the login.

Suggested fix (both sides):

- Server: give `device_token` its own limiter at the documented 20/min.
- CLI: treat 429 and `slow_down` as "wait longer" (increase the interval by 5s per RFC 8628 §3.5, honour `Retry-After`), and bound polling by the device code's `expires_in` rather than a fixed attempt count.

draft.title: [bug]: bifrost workflows execute hangs when the run finishes before the WebSocket subscribes
draft.body:
### Summary

`bifrost workflows execute` can hang forever after a fast successful run. If the run reaches its terminal status before the CLI subscribes to `/ws/execution/{id}`, the terminal event is never seen and the command never exits.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Register a workflow that completes very quickly (around 100 ms).
2. Run `bifrost workflows execute <ref>`.

### Expected behavior

The command prints the result and exits with status 0 (or 1 on failure).

### Actual behavior

The command prints `execution_id: ...` and then waits indefinitely, even though the execution shows `Success` on the server. It has to be killed.

### Environment

- `main` (also seen on a 1.4.2-dev CLI build)

### Logs / screenshots

Cause:

- `/ws/execution/{execution_id}` (`api/src/routers/websocket.py`) only sends `{"type": "connected"}` after subscribing. It never replays the current status.
- The worker publishes the terminal `execution_update` once. If that happens between the CLI's `POST /api/workflows/execute` and the WebSocket subscription, nobody receives it.
- `_stream_execution_logs` in `api/bifrost/commands/workflows.py` ignores `connected` and blocks on `recv()` waiting for a terminal update that will never arrive. The final GET that would backfill the result is never reached.

Suggested fix: when the CLI receives `connected` (the subscription is now live), GET `/api/executions/{id}` once and exit if the status is already terminal. This closes the race deterministically, because the worker commits the terminal status to the database before it publishes the update.

draft.title: [bug]: Deleting an OAuth integration leaves its tokens active; refresh job alerts on them every 15 minutes
draft.body:
## Summary

Deleting an integration that has an OAuth connection leaves its OAuth provider and tokens in place, and the `oauth_token_refresh` scheduler keeps refreshing them every 15 minutes, emitting `integration.refresh_failed` + `integration.reauth_required` on every run, indefinitely.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Create an integration and configure an OAuth (authorization_code) connection for it.
2. Complete the OAuth flow so a token with a refresh token is stored.
3. Delete the integration (`DELETE /api/integrations/{id}`).
4. Make the token unrefreshable (e.g. remove/revoke the app registration or grant at the provider).
5. Wait for the next `oauth_token_refresh` run (every 15 minutes).

## Expected behavior

Once an integration is deleted, its OAuth credentials stop being used: the scheduler no longer refreshes them, and no refresh events are emitted for it.

## Actual behavior

The deleted integration's token is still picked up on every scheduler run. Each failed refresh emits both `integration.refresh_failed` and `integration.reauth_required`, every 15 minutes, forever. The deleted integration is hidden from the integrations UI, so there is no way to disconnect the token and stop the alerts short of editing the database.

## Root cause

1. **Delete is a soft delete that leaves the OAuth rows behind.** `IntegrationsRepository.delete_integration` (`api/src/routers/integrations.py`) only sets `integration.is_deleted = True`. The linked `oauth_providers` row (client ID + encrypted client secret) and its `oauth_tokens` rows (encrypted access + refresh tokens) are untouched. `oauth_providers.integration_id` is `ondelete="SET NULL"`, but that never fires because the integration row is never removed.
2. **The refresh scheduler doesn't check `is_deleted`.** `run_refresh_job` (`api/src/jobs/schedulers/oauth_token_refresh.py`) selects every token that has a refresh token or uses client_credentials (or belongs to an MCP connection), without joining `integrations` or excluding soft-deleted ones.
3. **The UI can't reach it.** Every integrations list/get query filters `Integration.is_deleted.is_(False)`, so after deletion there's no UI path to disconnect the token.

As a side effect, a deleted integration's encrypted client secret and refresh token are kept indefinitely.

## Proposed fix

Both parts are needed: (1) prevents new orphans, (2) stops the alerts for orphans that already exist without a data migration.

1. **On delete, remove the OAuth credentials.** In `delete_integration`, clear `integration_mappings.oauth_token_id` for the integration's tokens, then delete its `oauth_tokens` and `oauth_providers` rows. The integration row itself stays soft-deleted, which matches the existing "a reused name is a new connection, never a credential revival" behaviour.
2. **In the scheduler, skip providers whose integration is soft-deleted.** Outer-join `integrations` on `oauth_providers.integration_id` and require `integrations.id IS NULL OR integrations.is_deleted IS FALSE`, so providers with no integration (MCP servers, standalone connections) keep refreshing.

Fix with E2E coverage is ready (each new test fails without the fix):
- `tests/e2e/api/test_integrations.py::TestIntegrationsCRUD::test_delete_integration_removes_oauth_credentials`
- `tests/e2e/oauth/test_token_refresh_deleted_integration.py::test_refresh_skips_tokens_of_deleted_integrations`

## Workaround

Find the orphaned tokens and delete them:

```sql
SELECT t.id AS token_id, t.status, t.status_message, p.provider_name, i.name AS integration
FROM oauth_tokens t
JOIN oauth_providers p ON p.id = t.provider_id
JOIN integrations i ON i.id = p.integration_id
WHERE i.is_deleted;
```

## Environment

- Observed on a live instance running **v1.4.1**: an integration with OAuth was deleted, and `refresh_failed` events then fired every 15 minutes from deletion onward.
- Root cause confirmed against `main` @ `c039ec36d`.

draft.title: [bug]: Solution publication times out while repeatedly scanning resolver cache
draft.body:
## Summary
Microsoft CSP Solution deployment repeatedly reaches the 15-minute server timeout after metadata commits and before the new app bundle activates. The observed production bottleneck is resolver-cache invalidation in the Python-source finalizer.

## Evidence
- Three failed jobs: ad88ce47-674f-45a3-bb39-1e9db8bfcde7, 40744282-48c1-4ff0-9a45-d806c1da8fd1, 2b009467-475e-48c2-bff0-7c53efafbcf7. An observed retry is 19829dd0-24b5-4797-be91-45ca450393a7.
- Package has 75 Python files and 150 runtime files, 1.3 MB. Latest completed retry used Kubernetes and 458 MB peak / 2 GiB memory limit.
- Read-only production diagnostics: DB idle in transaction after solution_file_index INSERT, no lock blockers; S3 list 0.337s and reads 0.04–0.069s; Redis PING 0.373s.
- Redis contains 90,650 keys. SCAN with COUNT 10 needed 7,073 requests / 6.073s for one resolver-name invalidation. COUNT 1000 needed 91 requests / 0.125s.
- set_module invokes invalidate_module_resolution_cache for every Python file; invalidation independently scans the entire Redis keyspace for each ancestor namespace. Hundreds of serial scans consume the deploy timeout.

## Expected behavior
Source refresh invalidates affected scoped resolver entries efficiently, preserves unrelated entries, and completes publication for this small prebuilt package.

## Proposed repair
Use an explicit practical SCAN batch size and a single resolver-prefix traversal per changed path, filtering affected logical names locally. Preserve immediate invalidation and cross-scope semantics. Add regression tests for nested/package names, unrelated scopes/names and scan count. Do not raise deployment deadlines to mask the bottleneck.

## Acceptance
Focused cache/storage tests pass and a representative large-keyspace check confirms scan requests are no longer multiplied by ancestor count. The platform fix must ship before the final CSP bundle can be accepted as published.

draft.title: [bug]: Dashboard charts crash with "K.default is not a constructor" after opening the code editor
draft.body:
## Summary

Dashboard charts crash with "K.default is not a constructor" if a Monaco editor was opened earlier in the same tab

## Steps to reproduce

1. Hard-load `/workflows` (any page without charts).
2. Open the code editor (`>_`) and open any file, e.g. `hello_world.py`.
3. Close the editor, click **Home**, then the **Dashboard** tab.

## Expected behavior

Dashboard renders its charts.

## Actual behavior

Error boundary: `K.default is not a constructor`. A hard refresh on the dashboard fixes it until the sequence above is repeated.

Control: hard-load `/dashboard` first, then open and close the editor. The dashboard keeps working. Only the order matters.

## Cause

- `client/src/lib/monaco-setup.ts` configures `@monaco-editor/react` to load Monaco from jsdelivr (`monaco-editor@0.54.0/min/vs`). That AMD loader installs a global `define` with `define.amd = { jQuery: true }`.
- Recharts depends on `decimal.js-light`, whose UMD wrapper checks `typeof define == "function" && define.amd` first. When that's present it calls `define(...)` and never sets `module.exports`.
- The bundler's CJS interop then yields an empty exports object, so `new Decimal(...)` (minified `new K.default(...)`) throws.
- The chart chunk (`CartesianChart-*.js`) is lazy-loaded and evaluated once, so it only breaks if its first evaluation happens after Monaco has loaded.

Verified by extracting the `decimal.js-light` factory from the shipped `CartesianChart-*.js` and running it in Node: with no global `define.amd`, `K.default` is the Decimal constructor; with `globalThis.define.amd` set, it's `{}` and `new K.default(10)` throws the same TypeError. In the browser, `window.define.amd` flips to `{"jQuery":true}` the moment a file opens in the editor.

## Suggested fix

Bundle Monaco instead of loading the CDN AMD loader, so no global `define` is ever installed:

```ts
import * as monaco from "monaco-editor";
import { loader } from "@monaco-editor/react";
loader.config({ monaco });
```

This needs Vite worker setup (`self.MonacoEnvironment.getWorker` with `?worker` imports) and adds to bundle size. It also removes the runtime dependency on jsdelivr, and the version mismatch between the `monaco-editor` dependency (^0.56.0) and the CDN pin (0.54.0).

Stopgap alternative: `delete window.define` once Monaco has initialised. Smaller, but brittle.

## Environment

- `ghcr.io/gobifrost/bifrost-client:latest` (`sha256:abafc84172166950ce8562fd5dcbeaf210ef54da6fc01ce1bea2c974f8c7bbb5`), unmodified
- main @ `ade714a`
- Chrome, macOS; Docker Compose deployment

---

_This issue was generated by AI (Claude Code) and reviewed by a human before posting._

draft.title: [chore]: #769 follow-ups: replace outdated worker Jobs on upgrade, and smaller leftovers
draft.body:
## Summary

Follow-ups from #769 (unified runtime; production reached the 1+x model on 2026-10-24 via #1044, #1045, #1048 and #1049).

### Replace worker Jobs running an older image (main item)

After an upgrade on Kubernetes, worker Jobs started before it keep running the old image until they retire. Idle extra Jobs retire after `pool_idle_seconds` (5 min), but the warm minimum only retires at `pool_max_lifetime_seconds` (6 h). That leaves up to 6 hours of old executor code running against the new schema and API, and no operator should have to act. In production on 2026-10-24 the warm Job was drained by hand (`begin_drain(incarnation, "rotated")`).

Fix: the worker controller compares each ready Job's image with the image it would launch now. For an outdated Job, it launches a current replacement, then drains the outdated one so its runs finish. It never deletes the Job, since the controller treats a missing Job as lost and fails its runs. Needs a unit test, plus a Kind drill: upgrade the image with a busy warm Job and confirm it is replaced without failed runs.

### Smaller leftovers

- **Static executors register `ready` too early.** Docker services or Deployments register `ready` and report an early, inflated budget while their pool starts (a minute or more cold), so the controller counts them as free capacity before they can claim. Register them `starting` and flip to `ready` after `PoolWorker._start_executor`. Planners (`launch_for_demand`, `largest_budget`, `block_services_that_never_fit`) should count only measured, ready executors.
- **Drop `ExecutionWorker.slots` and `scheduler_replicas.job_slots`.** They only serve older readers during a rolling upgrade; remove them next release with a forward migration.
- **Kind build experiment.** Its `--restart-scheduler` restarts the wrong process now that the API runs the build controller.
- **`WorkflowExecutionRequest.code`** is plain text, but its description says base64.

## Notes

- Handoff: `docs/plans/2026-10-22-769-handoff-status.md`.

draft.title: [chore]: Drop ExecutionWorker.slots and scheduler_replicas.job_slots after the next release
draft.body:
Split from #1052.

`ExecutionWorker.slots` and `scheduler_replicas.job_slots` only serve older readers during a rolling upgrade:

- v1.4.1 writes and reads `scheduler_replicas.job_slots` (Diagnostics heartbeat).
- Images built before #1052 read `slots` in `admit_worker` and refuse to start when it returns nothing.

No release has shipped since v1.4.1, so dropping either now would break the rolling upgrade from v1.4.1, or from the current dev images, to the next release. Drop both with a forward migration in the release after the next one (the first release whose predecessor no longer reads them), and remove `admit_worker`'s `RETURNING slots` and the remaining writes (`slots=0` in `_reserve` and `register_static_worker`, `job_slots` in `scheduler_diagnostics`).

draft.title: [feature]: Built-in workflow.completed topic for successful executions
draft.body:
### Problem

The built-in `workflow.failed` and `workflow.retry_exhausted` topics from #321 make it easy to react when a run fails, but there's no matching topic when a run succeeds. Anything that needs to act on a finished run has to poll execution status or add its own `events.emit()` at the end of every workflow.

Concrete example: we run a Microsoft Teams chat bridge. Someone asks for something in a chat, the bridge starts a workflow, and when the run finishes the bridge posts the result back into that chat. In our fork this relied on a fork-only `microsoft_teams.chat_run_completed` topic emitted by the platform. Moving to upstream, the options are polling, or adding an emit to every workflow the bridge can start. The second is easy to forget and never fires if the workflow fails before its last line. The same need shows up for completion notifications and simple chaining (run B after A succeeds).

### Proposed solution

Add `workflow.completed` to the curated registry in `api/src/services/events/registry.py`, and emit it from `api/src/jobs/consumers/workflow_execution.py` on successful completion through a helper in `api/src/services/events/builtins.py`, next to `emit_workflow_failure_events`.

The payload would mirror the existing `workflow.failed` body so subscribers can reuse input mappings:

```jsonc
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "occurred_at": "2026-05-28T12:34:56Z",
  "organization": {"id": "...", "name": "..."},
  "actor": {"type": "system", "id": null, "email": null, "name": "Bifrost"},
  "workflow": {"id": "...", "name": "sync_tickets"},
  "execution": {
    "id": "...",
    "attempt": 1,
    "max_attempts": 1,
    "status": "<terminal success status>",
    "started_at": "...",
    "completed_at": "...",
    "duration_ms": 1234
  },
  "trigger": {"type": "event", "event_type": "ticket.created", "event_id": "..."}
}
```

No inputs or results in the payload by default, so nothing new leaks through events. A subscriber that needs the result fetches the execution by id, which keeps the existing access checks and secret scrubbing in the path. Subscribers narrow it down with `filter_expression` (#653), for example by workflow name or trigger type.

Two things I'd want your call on:

- **Loop guard.** A workflow subscribed to `workflow.completed` produces its own `workflow.completed` when it finishes. `emit_event_delivery_retry_exhausted` already has a self-trigger guard; something similar could skip emitting for runs that were themselves triggered by `workflow.completed`, or it could be left to subscriptions plus docs.
- **Scope.** I'd keep this success-only to match the existing `workflow.failed` naming, rather than one generic terminal event for every status.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `workflow.completed` is in the curated topic registry with an example body
- [ ] Successful workflow executions emit it with the payload above; failed runs keep emitting `workflow.failed` only
- [ ] The payload contains no workflow inputs or results
- [ ] A workflow subscribed to `workflow.completed` can't trigger itself in an unbounded loop (guard or documented filter)
- [ ] Unit test for the body shape and an e2e test that a topic subscription fires on success
- [ ] `docs/events/topics.md` documents the built-in `workflow.*` topics (it only covers `user.invited` today)

I'm happy to implement this if it's wanted.

### Design doc link (optional)

_No response_

draft.title: [feature]: Opt-in strict validation for unknown manifest keys and @workflow kwargs
draft.body:
### Problem

Unknown keys are ignored silently in two places, and both are deliberate:

- `docs/plans/2026-02-04-workflow-decorator-simplification.md` makes unknown `@workflow` params warn, not error, for backward compatibility.
- Most manifest models in `api/bifrost/manifest.py`, including `ManifestEventSubscription` and `ManifestWorkflow`, use pydantic's default of ignoring extra fields.

I understand why, and I'm not asking to change the default. The cost shows up during migrations. Moving our workspace from a fork onto upstream:

- An event subscription still carried a legacy `criteria` key (our fork's filter field). Validation passed, the key was dropped, and the subscription matched every event on its source. It failed open with no signal anywhere.
- `retry_policy` and bounds kwargs on `@workflow` also validated as valid and were ignored. The decorator warning goes to the worker log, not to the validate result or push output the author is looking at.

This is the same class of problem as #652 (fixed in #653, where a stored `filter_expression` wasn't enforced), one layer up. The round-trip drift detector from #390 and #391 catches fields lost between export and import, but not keys the author wrote that the schema never knew about.

### Proposed solution

Two steps, with default behavior unchanged:

1. **Surface ignored keys as warnings.** The validate response gets a `warnings` list with the manifest path and key (for example `subscriptions[0].criteria`), and the CLI prints them on validate and push. Unknown `@workflow` kwargs get reported the same way, instead of only in the worker log.
2. **Opt-in strict mode** that turns those warnings into errors: a `strict` option on the validate endpoint and a matching CLI flag, and possibly a manifest-level setting. CI pipelines and migrations would turn it on.

This could be a validation-only pass that collects extras, so normal parsing and manifest round-trip stay exactly as they are. Some manifest models already use `extra="forbid"` (for example `ManifestWorkflowPermissionGrant`), so there's precedent for strict schemas where it's safe.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Default validate and push behavior is unchanged for existing workspaces
- [ ] The validate response lists unknown keys with their manifest path
- [ ] CLI validate and push print those warnings
- [ ] Unknown `@workflow` kwargs are reported the same way
- [ ] Strict mode fails validation on any unknown key
- [ ] Tests cover a subscription with an unknown key: a warning by default, an error in strict mode

I'm happy to implement this if it's wanted.

### Design doc link (optional)

_No response_

draft.title: Static launchers on non-k8s hosts: report version, rotate on build change, opt-in idle/N-run exit
draft.body:
We aim to run upstream main images on Docker Compose and want zero-downtime upgrades (no k8s tax yet), with Azure Container Apps as a scalable burst lane for workers. Static launchers are the natural fit for ACA, but they're defined as always-on and never replaced ([pool_main.py#L4-L6](https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/4b84c9474aa9a9e421a6af2db8a47b129780bf74/api/src/worker/pool_main.py#L4-L6), [#1052 plan](https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/4b84c9474aa9a9e421a6af2db8a47b129780bf74/docs/plans/2026-10-24-1052-replace-outdated-worker-jobs.md#L25-L30)). After an upgrade they keep claiming work on the old build, and they can't scale to zero.

This lines up with the thin-runtime roadmap item for demand-started launchers with a warm minimum and idle drain ([thin-runtime doc](https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/4b84c9474aa9a9e421a6af2db8a47b129780bf74/docs/benchmarks/2026-10-24-thin-runtime-live-jobs.md#L154-L160)). ACA is a concrete host for it, and so is Cloudflare Containers.

## Proposal

1. **Launcher reports its version.** Add the launcher's build to `Hello` ([protocol.py#L44-L53](https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/4b84c9474aa9a9e421a6af2db8a47b129780bf74/api/src/worker/remote/protocol.py#L44-L53)), and stamp the worker row with it. Today `register_static_worker` stamps the API's own version ([claims.py#L120](https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/4b84c9474aa9a9e421a6af2db8a47b129780bf74/api/src/services/worker_pool/claims.py#L120)).
2. **Retire outdated static launchers.** Extend `outdated()` and `replace_outdated()` ([controller.py#L95-L105](https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/4b84c9474aa9a9e421a6af2db8a47b129780bf74/api/src/services/worker_pool/controller.py#L95-L105)) to cover `form == "static"`, but only to mark them draining, since Bifrost can't start a replacement. The existing retire path already drains and exits cleanly ([launcher.py#L785](https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/4b84c9474aa9a9e421a6af2db8a47b129780bf74/api/src/worker/remote/launcher.py#L785)). The host's restart policy or scaler starts the replacement on the new image. Make this opt-in per launcher so warm-minimum installs keep today's behavior.
3. **Opt-in idle or N-run exit.** Add an env var, for example `BIFROST_STATIC_EXIT_WHEN_IDLE_SECONDS` and `BIFROST_STATIC_MAX_RUNS`. It would let a static launcher use the idle drain and lifetime gates it currently skips ([pool_main.py#L468-L481](https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/4b84c9474aa9a9e421a6af2db8a47b129780bf74/api/src/worker/pool_main.py#L468-L481)), and exclude those launchers from the `begin_idle_drain` warm-minimum count. That makes ACA Jobs or KEDA-style scale-to-zero possible.

**Out of scope:** the Job controller and the 300 s SIGTERM drain.

**Context:** this follows up our earlier ACA pilot, #242, against the current worker-pool architecture. We're happy to test on our staging instance.

draft.title: [bug]: Concurrent ordinary document merges lose disjoint updates
draft.body:
## Summary
Concurrent ordinary merges into the same table document can silently discard one writer's disjoint field changes. This affects partial update and the legacy merge-upsert path, without requiring a new CAS feature.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Create a document with `{"left": 0, "right": 0}`.
2. Session A merges `{"left": 1}` and flushes the UPDATE, holding its row lock without committing.
3. Session B has loaded the original document and starts the canonical ordinary update or legacy merge-upsert with `{"right": 1}`.
4. Confirm B is blocked on A using PostgreSQL `pg_blocking_pids`, then commit A and await B.
5. Read the stored document in a fresh session.

## Expected behavior
The final document is `{"left": 1, "right": 1}`. Each ordinary merge should construct its post-image from the current locked row. Existing pre-image and post-image policy checks must remain intact and see that same fresh row.

## Actual behavior
The final document can be `{"left": 0, "right": 1}`. The second writer computes a full JSON replacement from a stale ORM object before its eventual UPDATE waits for A's lock. Waiting at the UPDATE does not recompute that already-built post-image.

`api/shared/table_documents.py` reads with ordinary `get()` before merging. The existing-row branches in `api/shared/table_document_writes.py` also read before policy evaluation without acquiring and refreshing a write lock.

## Environment and reproduction results
- Unchanged upstream production code: `3aa8a7d9286f3894bd9b3978bea4a6e95d4378c8`.
- Latest main checked before filing: `4be06f5803ffc7820e69c8a1a410e5e84969a8a4`. Its two intervening changes affect worker templates and idle database churn, not the document repository/write paths.
- Real PostgreSQL/Redis repository-managed Docker test stack, synthetic UUID-scoped fixtures, two database sessions, no queued workflow jobs.
- Test-only commit `66ecdb38539a29456e1f66620ae6d8a01597f66e`: both parameterized regressions failed, one for each merge path.
- Candidate `fd4e0bd927f4a7062a805669bb98ae6c570b49b0`: 153 selected unit/e2e/API/policy/tenant/batch tests passed, API lint/types and Python CodeQL passed. Full suites and merge-queue checks have not been run locally.

## Smallest proposed repair and related history
Use PostgreSQL `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` plus SQLAlchemy `populate_existing=True`, scoped by the existing table/document filters, before policy evaluation and merge. Keep the existing transaction boundary. Same-row writers serialize, which can increase waiting on hot documents. No schema, API, dependency, CAS or batch-engine redesign is proposed.

Related #790 and #791 already fixed dual pre-image/post-image authorization. This is a distinct concurrent stale-image/lost-update regression, not a request to remove or reopen those checks. This report demonstrates data correctness failure, not an asserted security exploit.

draft.title: [bug]: Execution-log acknowledgement can erase uncommitted or unread logs
draft.body:
## Summary
Execution-log persistence can delete Redis source entries before the caller's PostgreSQL transaction commits, or delete a concurrent append that was never included in the persisted snapshot. Terminal cache cleanup can also erase retained/unread entries.

This is an execution-history correctness report. No security exploit, production incident or exactly-once delivery guarantee is asserted.

## Steps to reproduce
Use the repository-managed PostgreSQL/Redis test stack and the test-only reproducer identified below. It adds synthetic UUID-scoped executions, dispatches zero workflow jobs, and leaves production code unchanged.

```bash
./test.sh stack up
./test.sh tests/e2e/test_execution_log_durability.py -v --durations=0
```

Two discriminating cases:
1. Append an execution log to Redis. Call `flush_logs_to_postgres(..., session=caller_session)`, flush the database session, then roll it back. Inspect PostgreSQL and Redis in fresh reads.
2. Read the Redis snapshot through the real Redis client, append a second entry through an independent real producer before the flush continues, allow the owned-session database commit, then invoke normal terminal cache cleanup. Inspect persisted and unread entries.

## Expected behavior
1. Caller rollback leaves no committed log row, but preserves the Redis source. The flush must not commit unrelated caller work as a shortcut.
2. Successfully persisted snapshot entries may be acknowledged after commit, but the unread concurrent append must survive both acknowledgement and terminal cleanup.

## Actual behavior and current source
1. The caller-owned path only stages rows using `session.add_all`, then deletes the whole stream. A subsequent caller rollback leaves neither committed rows nor source entries.
2. Whole-key deletion removes an entry appended after the read snapshot even though that entry was not inserted into PostgreSQL. Terminal cleanup also deletes the whole log key, so fixing acknowledgement alone is incomplete.

At current main `30624cce04af01ab30a807ed4aa793c321ee5218`:
- `api/bifrost/_logging.py:509-591`: snapshot read, caller staging at573, owned-session commit at581, whole-key deletion at584.
- `api/src/core/cache/invalidation.py:342-358`: terminal cleanup includes `execution_logs_stream_key` in deleted keys.
- Existing completion consumers pass their transaction into the flush and commit later. Both success and failure completion paths need the same commit-before-ack ownership contract.

The owned-session commit-failure path already retains source, so this is not a claim that every database failure destroys logs.

## Reproducer and what actually ran
Test-only commit: `fef01d6049196d14b0b5ebc0d38cc88cdab706fc`, based on upstream `3aa8a7d9286f3894bd9b3978bea4a6e95d4378c8`, available on `Midtown-Technology-Group/bifrost` branch `repro/execution-log-ack-loss`.

On October 28, 2026, the above command ran in an isolated repository-managed Docker stack with real PostgreSQL and Redis: **3 failed, 2 passed, no skips/errors**. The two cases above demonstrate source loss. The third red case specifies failed exact-ID acknowledgement/replay behavior for a proposed repair, not a third independently established upstream defect. Controls cover owned-session commit failure and competing flushers.

Current main was inspected before filing. There is no diff from the tested production baseline in the three affected logging/cleanup/consumer files. No fresh execution on current main is claimed.

## Small repair direction, with an unresolved operational choice
A locally exercised candidate collects successfully parsed snapshot IDs, stages rows in the existing caller transaction, acknowledges only those IDs after commit, and preserves unacknowledged streams during terminal cleanup. It passed 68 focused tests, API lint/types and Python CodeQL. It is deliberately not presented as an upstream-ready repair yet.

Remaining tradeoffs to settle before a repair PR:
- Commit-before-ack is at-least-once: crashes or failed acknowledgements can replay committed rows. Existing database rows do not have a unique Redis stream ID, and sequence values are snapshot-local.
- Keeping empty Redis streams preserves their ID history but accumulates empty keys per execution. Current producers have MAXLEN10000, not an established expiry policy. MAXLEN bounds entries within a stream, not the number of keys.
- Deleting an empty stream resets its ID history. With competing stale acknowledgement batches and a recreated key, a reused ID can identify a new unread entry. Real Redis explicit-identical-ID tests demonstrate this structural risk, not the production frequency of an automatic same-millisecond collision. An atomic XLEN/DEL check only protects the append-versus-delete window, not identity reuse after recreation.
- Preserving unread source does not schedule eventual drain or prevent MAXLEN trimming. An invented TTL would merely choose a new silent-loss window.

Would you prefer the narrow at-least-once preservation repair with explicit empty-key retention, or should reclamation be tied to an existing authoritative execution-retention boundary? I would keep this separate from a new outbox, CAS contract, queue or replay-deduplication architecture.

## Related work checked
#972 fixes CLI completion-subscription timing, not source acknowledgement. #1068 preserves claimed workflows and reconciles event outcomes, not this Redis-to-PostgreSQL ordering. #925 sanitizes log messages, not persistence. Current all-state issue/PR searches found no direct duplicate. This report is independent of other table-document work and downstream migration.

draft.title: Fresh-install setup: explicit Secrets Reader path for the first administrator
draft.body:
## Problem

A fresh installation appears to leave its sole initial administrator without a supported self-service path to Secrets Reader.

The first-user provisioning path creates a Provider-organization Platform Admin, but does not assign Secrets Reader. Platform Admin intentionally excludes `secrets.read`, and the ordinary role-assignment UI/API prohibit changing your own roles. Another authorized principal can grant the role, but that assumes a second administrator is available.

I understand the separation is intentional: #869 requires explicit secret-access assignment, and #889 grants Secrets Reader only to administrators present during its migration. I'm not proposing that every new administrator automatically receive secret access.

## Source evidence

Inspected at `4f13ce8be901a8367d41da2388d92c47d26ac716`; targeted reads of current main on October 28 show the same provisioning and self-assignment behavior.

- [First-user provisioning](https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/4f13ce8be901a8367d41da2388d92c47d26ac716/api/src/services/user_provisioning.py#L100-L125)
- [User creation](https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/4f13ce8be901a8367d41da2388d92c47d26ac716/api/src/repositories/users.py#L119-L133)
- [Self-assignment restriction](https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/4f13ce8be901a8367d41da2388d92c47d26ac716/api/src/services/user_role_assignments.py#L542-L559)
- [One-time migration](https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/4f13ce8be901a8367d41da2388d92c47d26ac716/api/alembic/versions/20261003_r3_operator_secrets.py#L20-L35)

## Reproduction to add as a regression test

This is a source-derived reproduction, not a newly executed clean-install test:

1. Initialize an empty database through current migrations, then complete normal first-user setup.
2. Inspect the first user's authorization: Platform Admin is present, but explicit `secrets.read` is absent.
3. Attempt to assign Secrets Reader to that same user through the normal role-assignment surface.
4. Observe disabled self-edit in the UI / HTTP 400 from the API.

This concerns direct secret-dependent SDK access; it is not a claim that every workflow execution is blocked.

## Proposed direction

Could first-run setup offer an explicit, default-off Secrets Reader choice, with clear disclosure that the built-in role applies everywhere?

That choice should be tied to the verified first-user setup transaction, audited, atomic and non-replayable. Normal self-assignment restrictions, admin wildcard exclusions and role boundaries should remain unchanged. Later users/promotions should receive no automatic grant.

Regression coverage should include refusal/no grant, explicit consent/exact grant, concurrent setup and replay attempts, unchanged normal self-assignment denial, and no backfill of existing users.

Already-initialized single-admin installs also need a documented supported recovery path, or clear documentation that a second administrator is required. I haven't found a documented bootstrap option or an explicit decision rejecting one; if this case was considered, a pointer would help before implementing a fix.

draft.title: [bug]: Remote runner reconnect and cleanup can strand workflow execution
draft.body:
## Summary
Remote runner reconnect and failed test cleanup can strand workflow execution.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Start a remote session renewal and suspend its database result.
2. Reconnect the same physical launcher, advancing its session generation.
3. Complete the old renewal with a failed result. The current implementation acts on that obsolete result and loses the new session.
4. In the integration fixture, close the launcher before canonical drain completes. Its retirement wait fails; without unconditional restoration, later tests retain no workflow-capable executor.

The queue-exposed sequence is the two tests in `test_remote_runner_lifecycle.py`, followed by a workflow SDK test. It reproduced locally. A deterministic unit regression also reproduced the obsolete-renewal behavior.

## Expected behavior
An obsolete renewal must not change the current session. Fixture teardown must use the supported drain event, always stop the launcher, and restore executor capabilities even after a failure.

## Actual behavior
The queue logs show remote-runner teardown errors followed by a workflow timeout. A local cancellation reconnect also received a welcome and then a 1008 policy-violation close.

## Environment
Bifrost main at `2aaaaf811`; Docker test stack and merge queue. Exposed while merging #1028 and #1130; their App build-error and SSO changes do not cause the runner failure.

## Evidence
- [Build-error PR queue run](https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/actions/runs/40818512236)
- [SSO PR queue run](https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/actions/runs/40821198209)

The repair will be isolated in a maintainer PR so Will Spence's original PRs retain their scope and credit.

draft.title: Agent run stays running for ~35 min when its failure write meets a database outage
draft.body:
## What happens

An agent run in flight when the database or pooler restarts fails (`Connect call failed`). Its failure write in `AgentRunConsumer.process_message`'s exception branch (`api/src/jobs/consumers/agent_run.py`, the `except Exception` block that re-fetches the run and sets `failed`) runs during the same outage, fails, and is only logged (`Failed to update agent_run … after error`).

The row stays `running`. Nothing retries the write; `execution_cleanup._cleanup_stale_agent_runs` eventually marks it `timeout` after `max_run_timeout` (default 30 min) + 5 min grace. Users see a phantom live run for ~35 minutes, then a misleading "timed out" status instead of the database error.

## Evidence

Reproduced deterministically by the capacity harness pooler drills (Kind + CloudNativePG, PgBouncer Pooler deleted or SIGKILLed while a mixed load runs at 1/s) on `main` (16d2e45a5) and on #1139: the `agent-tools` run sent ~1 s before the fault was still `running` at the end of the 5-minute tail in all four runs.

## Direction

The outage lasts seconds. The terminal write should survive it: e.g. retry the terminal update with bounded backoff (within the run's claim/lease window) before giving up, so the row reflects the real outcome. Removing connection pre-ping (#1139) can make this path slightly more likely, since a stale pooled connection now fails one statement after a restart.

draft.title: Worker control socket reconnects with a new session generation on a transient database error
draft.body:
## What happens

When the API's worker-control websocket handler checks ownership (`owns_remote_session()` in `api/src/worker/remote/ownership.py`) during a database or pooler restart, the DB error closes the socket. The worker logs `Remote control connection lost; preserving local children` and reconnects with a new `remote_session_generation`.

Children are preserved and no executor is lost (verified), so this is churn rather than loss, but every brief DB blip regenerates every connected worker's remote session.

## Evidence

Capacity harness pooler drills (PgBouncer Pooler pod deleted, or pgbouncer SIGKILLed) on `main` (16d2e45a5) and on #1139: one worker's `remote_session_generation` changed in all four runs; no owner/leadership lease loss, no executor lost.

## Direction

Treat a transient DB error in the control loop's ownership check like the owner-renewal path after #1138: keep the session until its lease would actually expire, instead of closing the socket on the first error. Needs a careful review because it touches ownership fencing.

draft.title: [feature]: Add daily installation usage reporting
draft.body:
## Summary

Add default-enabled daily production installation and aggregate usage reporting to `POST https://reports.gobifrost.com/usage`.

## Expected Behavior

- Persist one random installation UUID per database across restarts and replicas.
- Send only the installation ID, version, previous completed UTC day, aggregate workflow and agent run counts, production environment marker, and schema version.
- Automatically exclude development, testing, debug, and unversioned builds.
- Support `BIFROST_USAGE_REPORTING_ENABLED=false` for staging/database clones and permanent opt-out.
- Reuse the existing elected scheduler and system configuration storage.
- Record successful delivery per day; delivery failures must not interrupt platform execution.
- Do not send customer identities, domains, installation URLs, prompts, workflow contents, credentials, or request metadata. The reporting application must not retain source IP addresses, user agents, referrers, or request headers; its Worker request logging must be disabled.
- Document the exact payload, defaults, privacy limits, and deployment controls.

## Acceptance Criteria

Focused tests cover the exclusion gates, UTC boundaries, retention rollups, persistent identity, duplicate suppression, and failed delivery. Test reports never contact the public receiver. Reports remain self-reported and unauthenticated, matching the accepted scope.

## Related Infrastructure

Receiver source is maintained separately in the private `gobifrost/cloudflare-infrastructure` repository. The sender belongs in the public Bifrost repository.

draft.title: [feature]: Keyless outbound auth via workload identity federation
draft.body:
## Problem
Workflows that call cloud or SaaS APIs usually authenticate with long-lived secrets stored in Bifrost, such as a service account key, a client secret or an access key. These secrets don't expire, they're painful to rotate, and a leaked one keeps working until someone revokes it by hand. Most mature platforms now let callers swap a short-lived signed identity token for short-lived access instead, including Google Cloud, Azure (Entra ID), AWS and HashiCorp Vault.

## Proposed solution
Add workload identity federation as a first-class credential type in the SDK and integrations:

- **Identity source.** Bifrost gets a short-lived OIDC token for its workload. This could come from the host it runs on (Azure managed identity, GCP metadata server, AWS, Kubernetes projected token, or a token file). Ideally Bifrost could also act as its own OIDC issuer, with per-integration audiences and claims, so it works on any host.
- **Exchange profiles.** Each provider defines how a token is swapped for access, for example Google STS with service account impersonation, an Entra federated credential, AWS `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`, or a Vault JWT role. New providers can be added without core changes.
- **Config.** An integration stores only non-secret values: the provider, the audience, the role or service account to use, the scopes, and an optional subject to act as.
- **Tokens.** Tokens are cached and refreshed inside the platform. Workflows ask for a credential and never see the exchange.
- Existing secret-based auth stays the default and doesn't change.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] An integration can reach at least two providers (for example Google and Azure) with no stored secret.
- [ ] Acting as another identity works where the provider supports it, for example Google domain-wide delegation through service account impersonation.
- [ ] Tokens are scoped per integration, refreshed before they expire, and never logged.
- [ ] A misconfiguration fails with a clear error and never falls back to another credential.
- [ ] Docs cover the trust setup on each supported provider.
- [ ] Unit tests cover the token exchange and refresh against mocked provider endpoints.

draft.title: RFC: Measure and improve execution queue fairness under mixed workloads
draft.body:
## Context

The PostgreSQL dispatch claim path already implements memory-fit backfilling and an anti-starvation guard. In `api/src/services/worker_pool/claims.py`, `claim_next()` selects the oldest compatible dispatch that fits currently free memory, but after `HEAD_OF_LINE_WAIT = 30s`, an older dispatch that fits the worker's *total* budget but not its current free budget blocks younger claims. `work_dispatch.py` separately reconciles unclaimed work with a 30-minute claim deadline. These are useful safety policies, **not** latency SLOs or class/tenant fairness guarantees.

Current references:
- [Claims and head-of-line guard](https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/main/api/src/services/worker_pool/claims.py)
- [Dispatch reconciliation and deadline](https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/main/api/src/services/work_dispatch.py)
- [Memory requests and learned sizing](https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/main/api/src/services/memory_requests.py)
- [Elastic execution roadmap (workflow lanes are future work)](https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/main/docs/architecture/elastic-execution.md)
- [Performance benchmark suite design](https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/main/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-27-performance-benchmark-suite-design.md)

## RFC question

Can the existing admission/dispatch policy bound interactive queue latency under mixed workloads **without starving large or background work**, and if not, what is the smallest compatible scheduling extension?

This RFC is **measurement-first**: do not introduce priority lanes, a second queue, or a new scheduler by default.

## Investigation

1. **Confirm exact policy and invariants on current main.** Trace claim ranking, dedicated-worker reservation, handler/version compatibility, dynamic memory budget, controller scaling, reconciliation, and process lifecycle. Verify whether the HOL `exists()` blocker can consider older work that this worker cannot handle; cover heterogeneous capacities/handlers and transaction races.
2. **Instrument before redesign.** Record durable enqueue-to-claim queue wait, p50/p95/p99 and oldest pending age by handler and (where safe) workload class/org; admission refusals split by insufficient free memory, hard pressure, HOL blocking, no compatible worker, and launch delay; queue-deadline failures and worker CPU/memory utilization. Keep cardinality bounded; avoid org/workflow IDs as metric labels.
3. **Run a reproducible mixed-load benchmark.** Include short human-facing executions, medium I/O-bound runs, CPU-heavy tasks, and long memory-heavy imports, with sustained arrivals as well as bursts. Test at least one fixed worker, heterogeneous workers, an elastic fleet, and artificially constrained memory. Include worker loss/cancellation and contention across organizations. Compare against no-background-load baselines.
4. **Explore alternative policies only if justified:** (A) current oldest-fit plus 30s guard; (B) bounded class-aware weighted/aging admission; (C) class-aware admission plus reserved or borrowable interactive capacity. Assess effects on bulk throughput, fairness and resource cost. Preserve durable PostgreSQL dispatch and existing memory admission, fencing, worker reservation and failure semantics.
5. **Separate scope:** `PlatformJob` checkpointing/yielding and full workflow continuation are related but independent design questions, not prerequisites to this RFC.

## Questions to answer

- Can interactive jobs wait behind an old large job despite fitting available memory? What is observed p99 impact?
- Can an incompatible/unlaunchable older dispatch trigger HOL blocking for a worker that could never execute it?
- Can sustained interactive traffic starve bulk jobs, or sustained bulk work exhaust interactive latency budgets?
- Does `SKIP LOCKED` or concurrency yield substantial overtaking or unfairness?
- Are CPU-bound jobs materially underserved by admission based only on memory?
- Does additional worker capacity solve the issue more cheaply and reliably than scheduling complexity?
- Which queue-wait/age measurements are currently exposed, and what gaps remain?

## Deliverables / acceptance criteria

- [ ] Source-linked description of the *implemented* scheduler, including SQL predicates and evidence-backed edge cases.
- [ ] Reproducible workload harness/results, with baseline and mixed-load p50/p95/p99 queue waits, execution latency, throughput, oldest age, timeout/failure rates, resource envelopes, and raw artifacts.
- [ ] Tests proving older jobs cannot block incompatible workers and verifying 30s aging, assigned-worker reservation, contention and cancellation behavior; fixes only if a concrete correctness defect is proven.
- [ ] Quantified decision record: keep existing policy, adjust HOL policy, introduce bounded workload-class fairness, or reserve capacity; state cost, risk and SLO tradeoffs.
- [ ] Follow-on implementation issues **only** for demonstrated gaps, explicitly avoiding parallel dispatch/scheduler subsystems.

## Non-goals

No immediate production scheduling rewrite, no blanket priority for all synchronous requests, no silently preempting/killing running workflows, no assertion of exactly-once external side effects, and no new infrastructure component just to implement queue priority.

draft.title: [bug]: Execution slide-out content lost its padding
draft.body:
## Summary

Execution details in the slide-out drawer lost their 16px content inset. The workflow name, status, and Result/Input/Logs inspector sit against the drawer edges.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open History and switch to Logs.
2. Select a log row to open its execution details.
3. Inspect the workflow heading and the Result, Input, and Logs tabs.

## Expected Behavior

Execution content has a consistent 16px inset from the drawer edges on desktop and phones, aligned with its header.

## Actual Behavior

The embedded execution details render without outer padding in the drawer.

## Cause and Repair

The UI modernization in #732 removed `p-4` from embedded execution details. The desktop history preview supplies its own padding, but ExecutionDrawer does not. Add the missing inset at the drawer host so other consumers retain their existing spacing.

## Validation

Extend the existing EXEC-04 browser happy path with rendered geometry checks for the workflow heading and inspector across all three tabs at 1440px and 390px widths. The focused run passed, as did 31 component tests, TypeScript, and ESLint (one existing warning in the review seed script).

draft.title: [bug]: Accepted chat runs appear failed after observation errors
draft.body:
## Summary
An accepted durable chat run is marked failed locally when subsequent WebSocket connection or replay fails.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Resolve createChatRun successfully.
2. Reject connectToChat or getChatRunState.
3. Observe sendMessage reject and a local failed run event.

## Expected behavior
Preserve the accepted server-owned run and offer restoration retry without resubmission.

## Actual behavior
Submission and observation share one catch, which emits a terminal failure for accepted work.

## Environment
Source baseline 6dde44b158e4de938db34c2cf129b0d12dacc4d2, React 19.3.1. Deterministic hook tests reproduce both cases; this was a source-review finding, not a React Doctor diagnostic.

## Validation
Both regressions fail on original source; corrected hook passes 19 cases, including retry, navigation and stale replay ownership.
draft.author: MTG-Thomas

draft.title: [bug]: Execution listeners register after effect cleanup
draft.body:
## Summary
Execution hooks can register listeners after their owning effect has been disposed.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Defer the WebSocket connect promise.
2. Unmount the hook or replace history scope.
3. Resolve the old promise.
4. Observe obsolete listeners registered after cleanup.

## Expected behavior
Disposed effects install no listeners or stale connection state.

## Actual behavior
Cleanup sees no listener yet; the async continuation registers it afterward, retaining obsolete callbacks or organization filters.

## Environment
Source baseline 6dde44b158e4de938db34c2cf129b0d12dacc4d2, React 19.3.1. Affects useExecutionStream, useNewExecutions and useExecutionHistory. React Doctor 0.9.21 no-set-state-after-await-in-effect supported this investigation; deferred tests establish the bug.

## Validation
Five regressions fail before the fix; corrected lifecycle suite passes nine cases. Shared WebSocket transport ownership is preserved.

draft.title: [feature]: Optional conditional streaming multipart copy
draft.body:
## Problem

BiFrost large copies rely on UploadPartCopy source conditions. Cloudflare documents these as unsupported on R2, while conditional ranged GetObject is supported. Earlier bounded R2 probes passed stale-source rejection; this is a documented support gap, not a demonstrated current data-loss bug.

https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/api/

## Proposed solution

Add explicit streaming multipart copy: pin source ranges by ETag, upload validated parts, and retain atomic conditional completion. Keep the default server-copy path.

## Acceptance criteria

- Preserve exact bytes, metadata/content headers and Expires.
- Reject source changes and incomplete ranges; abort on failure/cancellation.
- Preserve conditional destination publication and existing small-copy behavior.
- Document memory/egress tradeoffs and provider qualification limits.
draft.author: MTG-Thomas

draft.title: Support service authentication on worker-control WebSockets
draft.body:
Physical workers can authenticate their signed launcher hello, but cannot currently attach service-authentication headers to the preceding worker-control WebSocket handshake. That prevents deployments behind gateways such as Cloudflare Access Service Auth from using the existing physical launcher directly.

Add optional secret-backed handshake headers, leaving the default connection unchanged. Validate configuration before connecting, require WSS when credentials are present, refuse redirects and transport-header overrides, keep credentials out of wire/error logs, and exclude them from both execution-template environments. Preserve the existing signed hello, admission, ownership, reconnect and drain contracts.

This is platform source work only. It does not configure a gateway, create a credential, change a deployment, or replace the instance-wide signing secret with a scoped worker credential. The latter remains a separate security design concern.
draft.author: MTG-Thomas

draft.title: [RFC] Unattended run identities for Solution-managed workflows
draft.body:
## Problem

A deployed Solution cannot carry a custom run identity. `bifrost workflows update <ref> --run-as <identity>` returns `409 Conflict: Solution-managed entities can only be managed by deployment methods`, and the portable workflow manifest has no run-identity field.

As a result, scheduled and webhook-triggered Solution workflows run as the organization's default identity. On our upstream deployment that identity has Platform Admin but not Secrets Reader, so an integration read masks the OAuth token and Halo returns 401. Manual runs succeed because the operator has `secrets.read`.

## Current workaround

- Move the automation to loose Provider-org workflows.
- Create a dedicated Provider identity with Platform Admin + Secrets Reader.
- Set `--run-as` on each loose workflow.
- Use Provider-scoped loose tables instead of Solution-owned tables.

This works, but it gives up Solution ownership, requires duplicate definitions, and leaves a high-privilege identity outside the Solution lifecycle.

## Questions

1. How are others running unattended Solutions against upstream images when the workflow needs integration secrets?
2. Is the intended pattern to use a dedicated identity with Secrets Reader, or is there a platform mechanism we are missing?
3. Should `run_identity` be a portable Solution workflow manifest field, set on deploy?
4. Should the docs cover unattended identities, Secrets Reader, and the Solution run-as restriction? The current Workflows/Permissions pages only say workflows run as the executing user.

## Constraints

- Do not broaden Secrets Reader to the shared Provider default identity (162 workflows).
- Keep the automation reviewable and gated; apply remains off.

Happy to turn this into a docs PR or a platform proposal if that is the preferred path.

draft.title: [bug]: Expired platform jobs cannot recover after the last worker is lost
draft.body:
## Summary
A local PlatformJob can remain running indefinitely after the last physical worker is lost in a scale-to-zero deployment. The recovery function runs only inside worker claim loops, while capacity demand includes only queued jobs.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Use external managed capacity with warm workers set to zero and no static executor.
2. Start a native audit.query job and hold its handler behind a lock in a disposable database.
3. Remove its exact bound physical worker while the job is running.
4. Let its 30-second job lease expire with no other queued demand.

## Expected behavior
API-side control recovers expired leases according to the job's existing retry policy, making queued demand visible so replacement capacity can start. No manual enqueue or always-warm worker should be required.

## Actual behavior
The worker becomes lost/provider-deleted, but the job stays running at attempt 1 with an expired lease. In the live fixture, the lease expired at 16:33:10 UTC and was still expired/running at 16:36:30 UTC. No worker or queued demand remained.

## Environment and source evidence
Reproduced on unmodified upstream 457134dffb8ec7af12b0a9be437e66a3bc7b7400, version 1.4.2-dev.1793576391. Current main 3f79ac4fde18defc472b4e5ce83d43f881827125 still invokes recover_expired_platform_jobs only from PoolWorker._platform_job_loop. The shared capacity controller selects queued PlatformJobs for demand. With no executor, neither side can make progress.

## Proposed repair
Run the existing canonical lease-recovery function from API-side capacity/control reconciliation, independent of physical worker availability. Retain row-lock concurrency, recorded retry/cancel/failure policy and normal queue wakeups. Add a regression with no worker claim loop, plus focused existing lease/fencing coverage. No new job system, database schema, credentials or retry-policy change is needed.
draft.author: MTG-Thomas

The combined candidate passed the local pre-PR gate: 4,124 client tests, 11,516

not universal S3 parity or a full Azure platform matrix.

draft.title: [bug]: Windows CLI login credential exceeds Credential Manager blob limit
draft.body:
﻿## Summary

On Windows, a successful device-code login fails when the CLI serializes the complete connection credential into a single Windows Credential Manager entry exceeding the native generic-credential blob limit. Authentication succeeds, persistence fails with `(1783, CredWrite, The stub received bad data.)`, and the old expired profile remains selected.

## Observed evidence

- Target-served CLI: `1.4.2-dev.1793766440`; SDK contract3.
- Unmodified `bifrost.credentials.KeyringBackend.save` calls python-keyring's Windows backend with the complete serialized credential.
- Reviewed metadata-only tracing observed write1 (preserve existing index) succeed at150 UTF16 bytes, then write2 (new connection profile) fail at3328 UTF16 bytes with native error1783.
- Windows documents a maximum generic credential blob of2560 bytes: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wincred/ns-wincred-credentialw
- Official CLI session readback still resolves an expired token afterward.
- No token values, JWT identity claims or credential-store contents were logged or attached. No backend, account, storage permissions or server contracts were changed.

## Reproduction

Use synthetic credential strings whose serialized connection record exceeds1280 UTF16 code units. Exercise the actual KeyringBackend and Windows write adapter through an in-memory WinCred fake enforcing the documented byte limit. A3328-byte record reproduces the oversize native write. A live device login with a sufficiently large issued record reaches the same native failure after approval; live authentication is not needed for regression tests.

## Expected behavior

OS-protected Windows persistence supports realistically sized access/refresh credentials, or refuses before any mutation with a safe actionable size/stage error. Never fall back silently to plaintext, lose existing profiles, expose token values, or report complete login before persistence/readback succeeds.

## Fix acceptance

Preserve the existing OS-protected backend and multi-instance/legacy profile compatibility. Cover oversized records, Unicode byte boundaries, interrupted/partial writes, profile/index ordering, concurrent saves where applicable, readback, cleanup and safe diagnostics. Metadata must identify failure stage without secret values. Add synthetic regression tests; do not require real credentials or native live-store mutations. No server-side auth/contract change is needed by this report. Prepare a draft PR only; no merge or deployment is requested.

draft.title: Solution app builds ignore the shipped npm lockfile (except the SDK auto-update path)
draft.body:
## Summary

Solution app builds ignore the `package-lock.json` that ships with the app. Both the CLI prebuild and ordinary server-side builds run `npm install --package-lock=false`, so every deploy resolves a fresh dependency graph. The only locked path is the automatic SDK update.

## Impact

- **Reproducibility:** the same commit can install different transitive versions on different days, contrary to the repo's own `npm ci` / `--require-hashes` policy.
- **Speed:** measured 2.2-3.7x slower installs than `npm ci`.

## Where

- CLI prebuild runs `npm install --no-audit --no-fund --package-lock=false` then `npx vite build`: https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/1386e8cd57e93b2aa3f6ed92bfb61028c19b3937/api/bifrost/commands/solution.py#L1586
- The lockfile is already collected and shipped; `_collect_apps` excludes only `node_modules`, `dist`, `.vite` and similar: https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/1386e8cd57e93b2aa3f6ed92bfb61028c19b3937/api/bifrost/commands/solution.py#L1404
- `_materialize_local_app` writes the app and rewrites the `bifrost` dependency to the instance SDK URL: https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/1386e8cd57e93b2aa3f6ed92bfb61028c19b3937/api/bifrost/commands/solution.py#L1578
- Server builds default to the same unlocked install: https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/1386e8cd57e93b2aa3f6ed92bfb61028c19b3937/api/src/services/solutions/app_build.py#L225. `npm ci` is selected only when `require_lockfile=True`, which is set for the automatic SDK upgrade path (https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/1386e8cd57e93b2aa3f6ed92bfb61028c19b3937/api/src/services/application_build.py#L81), not ordinary deploys.
- The lock-refresh and graft implementation already exists for that path: https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/1386e8cd57e93b2aa3f6ed92bfb61028c19b3937/api/src/services/solutions/app_build.py#L283 and #L350.

## Measurements

App: `solutions/cloudflare-zone-inventory/apps/inventory`, 172 locked packages. Node 24.21.0, npm 11.19.0, Linux x64. Fresh temp dir per run, separate npm cache per variant. Single run each.

| step | `npm install --package-lock=false` | `npm ci` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| install, cold cache | 12.4 s | 3.3 s |
| install, warm cache | 5.4 s | 2.4 s |
| vite build, cold / warm | 2.8 s / 3.7 s | 4.4 s / 3.4 s |

Install is 3.75x faster cold and 2.25x warm. Build differences are run-to-run noise. Total cold install+build: 15.2 s vs 7.7 s.

Caveat: the SDK dependency was supplied as a local tarball rather than the CLI-injected instance URL, and this is one app with one sample per variant.

## Suggested change

- Use `npm ci` whenever a valid lockfile is present, in both CLI prebuild and server builds.
- Reconcile the injected `bifrost` entry through the existing `_refresh_sdk_lockfile` / `_graft_sdk_lock_entries` machinery instead of ignoring the lock.
- Execute the locked `node_modules/.bin/vite` when the lock is used, rather than `npx` resolving or downloading Vite.
- Fail clearly when the lock and manifest disagree; define behavior for apps without a lock.

## Acceptance

Lock-honoring on both paths; non-SDK locked entries preserved; SDK entry reconciled; clear failure on incompatible locks; unchanged behavior for apps without a lock.

## Non-goals

Switching package managers (pnpm/yarn) or the bundler.
draft.author: MTG-Thomas

draft.title: Reuse unchanged Solution app builds across CLI prebuild and server deploy
draft.body:
## Summary

Every app in a Solution bundle is rebuilt on every deploy. A one-file change rebuilds every app of that Solution, both in the CLI prebuild and, when no prebuilt dist is supplied, again on the server.

## Where

- The CLI prebuilds every source-backed app in a fresh temporary directory before the deploy request is sent: https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/1386e8cd57e93b2aa3f6ed92bfb61028c19b3937/api/bifrost/commands/solution.py#L1682
- The server appends a build spec for every bundled app regardless of change: https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/1386e8cd57e93b2aa3f6ed92bfb61028c19b3937/api/src/services/solutions/deploy.py#L1411
- A fresh deployment id is allocated even when a prebuilt dist is supplied: https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/1386e8cd57e93b2aa3f6ed92bfb61028c19b3937/api/src/services/solutions/deploy.py#L1484
- Server-side build list consumption: https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/blob/1386e8cd57e93b2aa3f6ed92bfb61028c19b3937/api/src/services/solutions/deploy.py#L1432

Any fix that only touches the server leaves CLI deploys paying the same npm/Vite cost. The reuse decision has to include the CLI prebuild.

## Proposal

- Compute a versioned build-input digest per app and persist successful provenance bound to the active deployment.
- On a validated hit, keep the existing deployment id and immutable dist instead of allocating a new one.
- Verify provenance and artifact presence before accepting a hit; anything unknown is a miss.
- Keep full Solution reconciliation, ownership checks, removals and source retention.
- Re-validate the expected active pointer during finalization; do not weaken that race guard for reuse.

## Cache key

Source + lock is not sufficient. Suggested versioned digest inputs:

- Canonically sorted relative paths and exact bytes of all materialized inputs, including binary/public assets and build configuration.
- Effective `package.json` after manifest dependency overrides, the lock, and the controlled SDK-lock transformation version.
- Exact SDK package content digest (the download URL is mutable and cannot identify content).
- Node/npm versions, OS/arch, install flags, build command/mode, non-secret build configuration.
- Actual Vite base path and app identity (the deployed app UUID derives from install + manifest UUID, so identical source in different installs is not automatically the same build).
- Builder/cache schema version.

## Correctness

- Same-instance, same-app reuse only initially; cross-install dedupe is a later project.
- Keep the original build timestamp and SDK metadata on reuse.
- SDK-only rebuilds must update the same provenance contract.
- A CLI preflight skip is a hint until the server validates; define conflict/fallback if the active deployment changes.

## Non-goals

Cross-install artifact deduplication, toolchain changes, export/import optimization.

draft.title: Promote Dev Images blocks main head: verifier cannot find 'E2E Tests (shard 3/3)'
draft.body:
## Summary

`Promote Dev Images` refuses the current `main` head because the verifier does not see the expected merge-queue job.

```
Refusing dev-image promotion:
  - required exact-candidate job 'E2E Tests (shard 3/3)' must appear once and pass; observed [None]
```

- Source: `1386e8cd57e93b2aa3f6ed92bfb61028c19b3937`
- Run: https://github.com/gobifrost/bifrost/actions/runs/41867684700/job/126706085197 (2026-11-04T16:29Z)
- Candidate image exists: `ghcr.io/gobifrost/bifrost-api:candidate-1386e8cd57e93b2aa3f6ed92bfb61028c19b3937`
- Promoted tag `sha-1386e8c` does **not** exist, so downstream consumers that pin promoted tags cannot take the head.

## Impact

Any CD lane that requires a promoted `sha-<7>` tag is stuck on the head until this passes. The commit is a security fix (patched Python and CA trust in container images), so the block also delays that fix.

## Likely cause

`api/scripts/verify_merge_candidate.py` requires a fixed list of ten candidate gate jobs, including `E2E Tests (shard 3/3)`. The merge-queue run for this SHA did not expose that job name (observed `[None]`), possibly because the E2E matrix or job naming changed, or the shard was skipped on `merge_group`.

## Ask

Either align the verifier's required job list with the current E2E matrix, or fix the merge-queue run so the `E2E Tests (shard 3/3)` job appears. Please also confirm whether a rerun of the promotion is safe once corrected.
